entries.name: Fight as a group: duos, quads, kiting, tower draining
entries.title: Fight as a group: duos, quads, kiting, tower draining
entries.summary: How players fight in formation. A duo is an attacker with a healer on the next tile; a quad is four creeps in a 2 × 2 block, where every creep reaches every other with 12 per HEAL part. The tables give the HEAL parts a group needs under tower fire, the damage its parts deal and the CPU its intents cost.

steps.text: Scout the target: number of towers, where they stand, rampart hits, safe mode. The first table turns towers and range into the HEAL parts that must stand next to the creep under fire.

Pick the size. Community practice knows two formations: the duo, one attacker or dismantler with one healer behind it, and the quad, four creeps in a 2 × 2 block. Take the duo where one healer covers the fire (first table), the quad where it does not or where the fire moves between creeps.

Bodies: TOUGH first, HEAL last, and the same share of MOVE in every member. RANGED_ATTACK and HEAL in one body both work in the same tick. ATTACK or WORK next to HEAL do not, so melee and dismantle creeps leave the healing to their partner.

Decide on boosts for the whole group, not per creep. Unboosted, four bodies hold at most 100 HEAL parts beside their MOVE parts, 1200 per tick: the close-range fire of 2 towers, with no part left to attack.

Duo on the move: the leader follows the path, the follower calls move(leader) and steps onto the tile the leader leaves. With leader.pull(follower) the pair cannot tear apart; the fatigue of the follower then lands on the leader.

Quad on the move: search one path for the top-left creep, with a cost matrix in which a tile is as bad as the worst tile of its 2 × 2 block (wall or structure: blocked; swamp: swamp cost). Give all four the same direction in the same tick, and only when all four have fatigue 0. Through a gap one tile wide go in a line and form up behind it.
Every tick each creep with HEAL parts heals: the member that lost hits, else the member the defence will most likely hit next (pre-heal).
Every tick each creep with RANGED_ATTACK parts shoots: rangedAttack on the common target, rangedMassAttack when the targets in range add up to more and no ally stands close.
Kiting: against melee creeps hold range 3 and step back when they reach range 2. It works only while your creep moves every tick: enough MOVE for the terrain behind it, and no swamp on the way back.

Tower draining: stand at range 20 or more from the towers, next to an exit, with the healing for that fire. Each shot costs the defender 10 energy; when hits fall, step onto the exit tile and heal up in the next room.
Fix the retreat rule before the fight: leave when the damage of one tick exceeds what the group heals, when the boosted TOUGH parts are gone, or when a member is lost.

tasks: how to fight as a quad
how many heal parts does a quad need
pitfalls: move() returns ERR_TIRED while the creep has fatigue. One tired member stops or splits the formation: check the fatigue of all members before any of them moves.

rangedMassAttack hits every creep and structure in range that has an owner other than you, allies included, and nothing without an owner: walls, roads and containers take no damage from it. Use rangedAttack on a wall.

A creep that ends a tick on an exit tile is in the next room one tick later. A formation that crosses a border is split over two rooms for that tick; cross where no enemy waits, and form up two tiles inside.
Boosted TOUGH lowers damage only while those parts have hits. Once they are gone the same fire lands in full, and the HEAL parts behind them are next.
Each move, heal and ranged attack is an intent of 0.2 CPU; a quad that moves, heals and shoots pays 2.4 CPU per tick before any path search (third table).
notes: heal works at range 1 with 12 per part, rangedHeal up to range 3 with 4. In a 2 × 2 block all four creeps are within range 1 of each other, so all their HEAL parts can go to one member at full strength.

A heal is added to the target without asking whether it has lost hits, and is settled against the damage of the same tick. A heal on a full creep that is hit in that tick counts in full: pre-healing rests on this.
heal drops attack and dismantle of the same creep in that tick; rangedAttack and rangedMassAttack still run. rangedHeal drops all four.
A creep may enter the tile that another creep leaves in the same tick. That lets a follower take the leader's tile and a block shift as one.
rangedAttack reaches range 3, attack range 1: two free tiles between a ranged creep and a melee creep keep it out of reach for one more step.
rangedMassAttack does 10 / 4 / 1 per part to each target at range 1 / 2 / 3. It beats one rangedAttack from 2 targets at range 1, 3 at range 2 or 11 at range 3.
A tower shot costs 10 energy and a full tower holds 100 shots. From range 20 each shot does 150.
Community practice: draining pays against a room that refills its towers slowly or shoots at everything. A defender that holds fire while its towers cannot beat the healing is not drained.
Community practice on the other side: defenders spread tower and creep fire over the members of a quad instead of one target, so that its healing has to split.

entries.name: Organise creep logic: roles, tasks or a kernel
entries.title: Organise creep logic: roles, tasks or a kernel
entries.summary: Three ways players structure the code that drives creeps: a role per creep that decides for itself, a manager per room that hands tasks to general creeps, and a kernel that runs everything as processes with priorities. They differ in where a decision is made and what it costs in CPU and code; the game allows all of them and charges the same 0.2 CPU per intent.

steps.text: Roles, the way of the tutorial: give each creep a role name in its memory when you spawn it, and every tick call the module of that role for the creep. One module per job, one body per job.
Inside a role keep a state in memory (for a hauler: collect or deliver) and change it only when the store runs empty or full. A creep that decides anew every tick flips between jobs.
Lock targets: store the id of the chosen target, fetch it each tick, check cheaply that it still fits (exists, not full, still damaged), and search again only when it does not.
When several creeps repeat the same search, move the decision up: a manager per room collects the work once per tick (sites, structures to fill, things to repair) and hands each free creep a task.
A task is data: action, target id, range. The creep code only moves into range and calls the action, so one general body (WORK, CARRY, MOVE) can take whatever is needed next.
The two combine: fixed posts such as the miner at a source stay roles; hauling, building and repairing go out as tasks.

A kernel, when run order and CPU get hard to manage: wrap each piece of logic (a room, a remote, the market) as a process with a priority. A scheduler runs them in order, stops at a CPU budget, and raises the priority of what had to wait.
In any structure: tie optional work to the bucket, and wrap each creep or process in try/catch so that one error does not end the tick for all.

tasks: how do I organise creep roles
lock a target instead of searching every tick
pitfalls: An error that nothing catches ends the loop for the tick: every creep after the failing one does nothing. Catch per creep or per process and log the stack.
A loop that runs past Game.cpu.tickLimit is cut where it stands, so whatever comes last is skipped on such ticks. Order the work so that the last part is the one you can do without.

Without a memory option a new creep takes over the Memory.creeps entry that a dead creep of the same name left behind, old role and old target included. Pass the memory with every spawnCreep or delete the entries of dead creeps.
Process state kept only in the global scope is lost on every reset. Keep in Memory what a process cannot work out again, and rebuild the rest.
notes: creep.memory is Memory.creeps[name]. A role or task stored there is found again after a global reset; one held only in a variable of the global scope is not.
spawnCreep writes its memory option into Memory.creeps[name] in the tick of the call, so role and home room are set before the creep exists.
Game.getObjectById returns null for an object that is gone or in a room you do not see. A locked target needs that check every tick.
The fee of 0.2 CPU per intent is the same in every structure. What the structure changes is the CPU spent on deciding, not on acting.
Community practice: role creeps are built for one job and are cheap for it. When the job runs out they stand idle unless the role says what else to do.
Community practice: general creeps with tasks follow what the colony needs and spare the repeated checks of many equal roles. The price is larger, less fitted bodies and a manager to write.
Community practice: target locking spreads the cost of choosing over many ticks. It gains only when the check of the stored target is cheaper than the search.

Community practice: a kernel pays late, when CPU is the limit and priorities must decide what a short tick drops. Before any game logic it needs process ids, a process table and state that survives a reset.

entries.name: Cut the cost of Memory: smaller data, MemHack, own serialisation
entries.title: Cut the cost of Memory: smaller data, MemHack, own serialisation
entries.summary: Memory costs CPU twice in a tick: JSON.parse of the whole string at the first access, and JSON.stringify of the whole object after the loop. Players cut that by storing less, by keeping the parsed object in the global scope (MemHack, which rests on an internal of the runtime that may change), or by doing the serialisation themselves through RawMemory.

steps.text: Measure first. RawMemory.get().length is the size in characters (limit 2,097,152). Read Game.cpu.getUsed() before and after the first touch of Memory for the parse, and time JSON.stringify(Memory) once for the save, which no reading inside the loop shows.
Store less: delete the Memory.creeps entries of dead creeps, keep ids instead of objects, drop what can be worked out again.
Flatten what stays: a position as one short string or number instead of {x, y, roomName}, a path as the string of Room.serializePath, a list of ids as one joined string.
Move bulk that is read seldom (room intel, statistics, serialised cost matrices) into segments. A segment is a plain string: it costs nothing until you parse it yourself.
Keep derived data in the global scope and rebuild it after a reset: recipe:cache-between-ticks.

MemHack, when the parse still costs too much: in the first tick of a global read Memory as usual and keep the object in a module-level variable. In every later tick, before anything else touches Memory: delete global.Memory; global.Memory = saved; RawMemory._parsed = saved.
A riskier step on top: set RawMemory._parsed only every N ticks, so that the stringify runs only then. Everything changed since the last save is lost when the global resets.

Or serialise yourself: decode RawMemory.get() in your own format, work on your own object, and hand the new string to RawMemory.set() at the end of the loop. In such a tick use neither Memory nor creep.memory nor the stored path of moveTo.

tasks: skip the memory parse every tick
what does memory cost per tick
save memory only every few ticks
pitfalls: In the first tick after a global reset the saved variable is empty. Use the normal Memory in that tick and take the reference from it; putting undefined on global.Memory breaks every memory shortcut.

With RawMemory._parsed unset nothing is stringified and the stored string stays as the last save left it. A reset between two saves throws away every change since: creep memory, spawn bookkeeping, all of it.
A read of Memory after RawMemory.set() in the same tick parses your string and the runtime writes its own JSON over it. Decide per tick which of the two you use.
A stored string that is not valid JSON makes Memory null for the tick, and every Memory.x and creep.memory then throws. With an own format, stay away from the Memory object altogether.
notes: Each tick the runtime defines Memory on global as a getter. The first read runs JSON.parse on the stored string, keeps the result in RawMemory._parsed and puts that object in place of the getter.
After the loop the runtime stringifies what RawMemory._parsed holds, if it holds anything. The CPU clock stops after that, so the save is charged to you.

MemHack rests on two things the API reference does not promise: Memory is a configurable property of global, so it can be deleted and set, and the save reads RawMemory._parsed. Either may change with a server update; build a switch that turns the hack off.
MemHack saves the parse only. The stringify after the loop still runs every tick, in proportion to the size of Memory.
creep.memory, room.memory, flag.memory and spawn.memory look up global.Memory at each access, so they work on the object you put there.
RawMemory.set() stores your string as it is and drops the parsed object, so the runtime does no stringify of its own. The string may have 2,097,152 characters.

The official caching article gives the same advice on size: objects cost more to parse than strings, turn positions into flat strings, compress large repetitive data such as cost matrices and keep the unpacked copy in the global scope.
Community practice: MemHack is the usual name for keeping the parsed Memory in the global scope; the wiki page that describes it calls it a hack that may stop working.

entries.name: Profile CPU and keep long-term statistics
entries.title: Profile CPU and keep long-term statistics
entries.summary: Beyond single readings of Game.cpu.getUsed(): wrap functions to see where the CPU goes, write a few numbers per tick into Memory or a segment, and let a tool outside the game collect them into graphs. The official third-party page lists the profilers and statistics tools; the bucket tells what a tick was really charged.

steps.text: Begin with coarse blocks as in recipe:measure-cpu: per room, per role, per process. Go deeper only where a block is large.

Function profiler: put wrappers around prototype methods and your own functions that read getUsed() before and after and add up calls and CPU per name. Switch it on from the console for a set number of ticks, print the table, switch it off: the wrappers cost CPU themselves.

Take the true cost of a tick from the bucket: charged CPU = Game.cpu.limit − (bucket now − bucket one tick before). It holds while the bucket is below its cap and no pixel was made, and it includes the Memory save.
Pick a small set of numbers per tick: CPU used and charged, bucket, heap, global resets, creeps, energy in storage per room, progress of controllers and of the account level.
Put them where a collector can read them: one object under Memory that is overwritten every tick, or JSON in a segment, which adds nothing to the Memory parse.

Collect outside the game: an agent with an auth token reads that place over the web API on a timer and feeds a time-series store with a dashboard. Give the token access to that endpoint or segment only.
Without outside tools: print a summary to the console every N ticks, or draw the last ticks as a graph with room visuals from an array kept in the global scope.
Add alarms for what must not wait for a look at a graph: a bucket that stays low, a room without a spawn. Group them so that one fault does not send a mail per tick.

tasks: which function uses the most cpu
how much cpu was the last tick charged
pitfalls: A wrapper around a method that queues an intent books the 0.2 fee to that method, so Creep.move looks costly although its run time is small. Count intents apart from run time.
A wrapper must pass arguments and return value through, and must not be put on twice. The official prototype article shows the pattern with a guard.
Statistics kept in Memory are parsed with it every tick. Overwrite one object instead of appending history; history belongs in a segment or in the outside store.
The first tick after a global reset compiles and loads every module. Record resets as a number of their own instead of letting them lift the average.
notes: Kinds of tools on the official third-party page: a profiler that wraps functions (screeps-profiler), collectors that feed Grafana or Kibana (ScreepsPlus Grafana, screeps-grafana, screeps-stats), and statistics that stay in the console (screeps-ConsoleStats).
The same page warns: never give a third party your password, many tools rest on unofficial APIs and may stop working, and none are reviewed by the developers.
getUsed() is the CPU time of your isolate since the loop began plus 0.2 per queued intent. The Memory save comes after the last reading you can take.
After a tick the bucket is bucket + limit − charged CPU, cut at the bucket size. Two bucket readings one tick apart therefore give what the tick between them was charged, rounded up to a whole CPU.

Official limits for requests with a token: GET /api/user/memory 1440 per day, GET /api/user/memory-segment 360 per hour. That is one read per minute or one per 10 seconds; when ticks are faster, keep the last ticks inside the object the collector reads.
Community practice: compare relative numbers only. The same code reads differently on the official server and on a private one, and the simulation gives no usable CPU reading at all.
Community practice: graphs over days show what watching cannot: energy lost while a room changes level, CPU use that creeps up, a bucket that slowly drains.

tables.title: CPU per tick that intents alone cost
head: creeps
1 intent each
2 intents each
3 intents each
3 each, over 1500 ticks
tables.foot: 0.2 CPU for every call that returns OK. A profile shows this share under the methods that queue intents; faster code does not shrink it, fewer calls do.

entries.name: Toolchain: typings, bundler, uploader, starter kit
entries.title: Toolchain: typings, bundler, uploader, starter kit
entries.summary: The server runs plain JavaScript modules with flat names. Everything else players use (TypeScript, folders, npm packages, other languages, automatic upload) is a build step on their own machine that ends in one upload of modules. The official third-party page lists the common tools; the developers review none of them.

steps.text: Ask whether you need a build step at all. The editor in the client, the folder sync of the Steam client and plain JavaScript modules work without one.
Typings: a package of declarations for the game API gives the editor completion and, with TypeScript, type checks before upload.

Language: TypeScript is compiled to JavaScript. Python and Kotlin are translated to JavaScript by their starter kits. Rust, C and C++ are compiled to WebAssembly and uploaded as a binary module next to a small JavaScript loader.
Bundler: joins your folders and npm packages into one main module and leaves out what is not used. Without one, flatten folder paths into module names (lib/util.js becomes lib_util) in a copy step.
Uploader: a task that posts the built modules to a branch with an auth token; recipe:upload-code has the request. Keep one target per server: main world, PTR, season, private server.
Starter kit: a repository in which typings, build and upload are already wired together. Take one for your language, then read its configuration before you trust it with a token.
Keep the token in a file that is not committed, and give it only the access the upload needs.
Tests: run pure logic (body builders, planners, queues) on your own machine against mocks of the game objects; run the whole bot on a private server or the PTR.

tasks: bundle my code into one file
starter kit for a new bot
write my bot in rust or python
pitfalls: Every upload throws the global scope away: the next tick loads all modules again and finds every cache empty. A watch task that uploads on each saved file causes a reset each time.
The whole bundle is compiled in the first tick after each reset, on your CPU. Packages that are bundled but not used cost on every reset.

The error you get is the stack of the modules as they were uploaded: after bundling it points into the bundle, not into your source files. A source map can translate it; load it only when an error occurs, since it takes heap and CPU.
A compiler that renames property names breaks calls into the game API; the official page lists externs for that case. Leave the names of game objects and constants alone.
notes: The runtime knows only module names: require strips a leading "./" and looks the name up among the uploaded modules. There are no folders on the server.
A binary module comes back from require as its bytes; that is how WebAssembly built from other languages gets in.
lodash is built in, as the global _ and as require("lodash"). A bundler that packs its own copy makes the bundle larger for nothing; mark lodash as external.

The official third-party page names the tools of the table below, and warns that they rest on unofficial APIs, may stop working, are not reviewed by the developers and must never be given your password.

The contributed grunt article shows the usual extras of a build: credentials in a file kept out of git, the branch chosen on the command line, folders flattened into module names, a version stamp in the code, upload to a private server.
Community practice: the ways players push code are the editor in the client, the synced local folder, the GitHub sync, the web API driven by a task runner, and a bundler with an upload step.
Community practice: starter kits and typings for more languages than the official page names are collected on the links page of the wiki.

entries.name: Extend game prototypes and add console helpers
entries.title: Extend game prototypes and add console helpers
entries.summary: A method or getter added to Creep.prototype, Room.prototype or another game class is there on every object of that class and stays until the next global reset. Players use this for shortcuts, cached lookups, wrapped built-in methods and commands to type in the console.

steps.text: Put all extensions into modules that main requires at its top, outside the loop. They then run once per global reset, not once per tick.
A new method: assign a function to the prototype of the class. Inside it, this is the object the method was called on.

A new property: Object.defineProperty on the prototype with a get function and configurable: true. Keep the computed value on the object under another name; it is then computed once per tick and object.
A value that should outlive the tick: keep ids in Memory or in the global scope and turn them into objects inside the getter.

Wrap a built-in method: keep the original under a new name, but only if that name is still free; then put a function in its place that does your extra work, calls the original with the same arguments and returns what it returned.

Console helpers: assign functions to global, or call your prototype methods on objects from the console (Game.rooms.W1N1.myReport()). Give global helpers a common prefix so they do not collide with later code.
Keep a list of what you changed. After an update of the game, compare your wrapped methods with the new behaviour.

tasks: add a method to all creeps
pitfalls: The engine calls its own methods through the prototype: moveTo calls moveByPath, and moveByPath calls move. A replaced move changes all three; keep arguments and return codes as they were.
A wrapper installed twice wraps itself and never reaches the original. Store the original only when it is not stored yet.
A game object keeps each property value from its first read. One held over in the global scope answers with the values of its own tick; cache the id and fetch the object again.

Helpers on global and prototype changes are gone after a reset until the module runs again. Defined inside the loop they are redefined every tick for nothing; defined in a module that is never required they do not exist.
A getter that reads Memory (a memory property on sources) triggers the Memory parse like any other access.
notes: The game classes are made once per isolate. A change to a prototype stays until the global reset, and comes back when your module runs again after it.
Game objects are created anew every tick, so a value kept on the object itself is gone in the next tick.
Every game object gets its own RoomPosition, made with new. Two positions for the same tile are different objects: a value cached on one is not on the other.
Game is a plain object built new each tick, not a class. What you assign to Game is gone next tick, and there is no prototype of it to extend.
A console command is evaluated in the global scope of your script after the loop, so functions on global and methods on prototypes can be typed there.

The official contributed article walks through the patterns: adding methods, keeping the original before overwriting, passing arguments on, getters with a cache for the tick and with a cache in Memory, and a memory property for sources.
Community practice: prototypes for behaviour that belongs to one object (an own movement method on creeps, the sources of a room), functions on global for commands.

entries.name: Incoming nuke: protect, evacuate, rebuild; and where to aim one
entries.title: Incoming nuke: protect, evacuate, rebuild; and where to aim one
entries.summary: A nuke shows in FIND_NUKES for 50,000 ticks before it lands. Players use that time to choose, structure by structure, between a rampart that takes the blast (50,000 energy per tile in the outer ring, 100,000 on the centre tile) and rebuilding afterwards, and they move every creep out of the room before the landing tick.

steps.text: Detect: room.find(FIND_NUKES) in every owned room, every few hundred ticks. Each nuke gives pos, timeToLand and launchRoomName. Store them and notify yourself.
Map the blast: 10,000,000 on the target tile, 5,000,000 on each of the 24 tiles within range 2. Add up per tile over all nukes aimed at the room.
Choose per structure with the table: a rampart where rebuilding costs more or where the contents must survive (storage, terminal, labs, factory); let cheap structures go and rebuild them.
Raise the chosen ramparts to the summed blast plus a margin: 50,000 ticks of one WORK part per outer tile, 100,000 for the centre. A creep with 20 WORK needs 2500 ticks per outer tile.
Empty what you leave unprotected. Carry the contents out of the blast or send them away through the terminal before the landing.
Before the landing: move all creeps into a neighbouring room, let no spawn be busy (a body of 50 parts takes 150 ticks), place no construction sites.
After the landing: bring the creeps back, place the sites again, refill the towers. For 200 ticks the controller takes no upgrade and no safe mode; expect the attacker's creeps in that window.

Aiming one yourself: choose the tile whose range 2 covers the most of spawns, towers, storage and terminal; read the rampart hits with an observer shortly before; send several nukes at one tile when a rampart holds more than one blast; let your creeps enter after the landing tick.

tasks: what to do when a nuke is coming
rampart hits needed against a nuke
move creeps out before a nuke lands
is it cheaper to rebuild after a nuke
pitfalls: The nuke strikes in the tick in which timeToLand reads 1. Creeps must have left by then; a repairer that stays to finish a rampart dies with what it carries.
A landing does not hand you a fresh safe mode at once. The cooldown is cleared only when the nuke ended a running safe mode, and for 200 ticks the blocked controller refuses activation either way.
Your own nuke kills your creeps in the target room as well. Keep the attack force outside until the tick after the landing.
A launch costs 300,000 energy and 5000 ghodium and the nuker then waits 100,000 ticks; the defender sees the target tile for 50,000 ticks and can raise ramparts exactly there.
notes: A rampart takes the blast first, and only the damage above its hits reaches what stands under it. Hits equal to the blast are enough; the rampart is gone afterwards.
Every nuke is worked off by itself: two on one tile need a rampart worth both blasts.
All creeps in the room die in the landing tick, under a rampart or not. Construction sites, dropped resources, tombstones and ruins are removed, and a spawn loses the creep it is making.
A structure destroyed by a nuke leaves no ruin: what it held is lost with it.
The landing ends a running safe mode and blocks the controller for 200 ticks. While the block lasts, activateSafeMode does nothing.
A rampart can hold 3,000,000 hits at room level 4 and 10,000,000 at level 5. Below level 5 no rampart takes even the blast of the outer ring.
Until the landing a rampart loses 150,000 hits to decay. Add that, or finish the repair late.
Community practice: defenders answer a launch at once, with ramparts under the valuable structures in the blast, and keep their creeps in another room until the nuke has landed.

Community practice on the attack: a nuke reaches the middle of a base without a breach, thins ramparts before creeps arrive and empties the room of defenders. Walls several layers thick are a favoured target.

tables.title: Rampart or rebuild, per structure in the blast
head: structure
energy to rebuild
rampart for the outer ring
rampart for the centre tile
cheaper in the outer ring
tables.foot: Rampart energy: the blast times 0.01 energy per hit, for a rampart built up from nothing; one that stands needs only the difference. Rebuilding also costs what the structure held and the ticks until it works again.

entries.name: Debug by looking: say, room visuals, map visuals
entries.title: Debug by looking: say, room visuals, map visuals
entries.summary: Three ways to see what the code thinks, each lasting one tick: a speech bubble over a creep (10 characters, no intent fee), drawings in a room (up to 500 KB per room and tick) and drawings on the world map (up to 1000 KB per tick). Players show creep states, paths, targets and plans with them.

steps.text: State of a creep: say() a short code or one icon per state (harvest, haul, build, flee). Any Unicode character works.
Paths: pass visualizePathStyle to moveTo while you debug movement, or draw a stored path with RoomVisual.poly.
Numbers where they belong: text next to a structure for its energy or queue, next to a source for the miner assigned to it, next to the controller for progress per tick.
Targets and plans: a circle on the tile a creep is locked on, a mark on the planned tile of each structure, the tiles of a cost matrix above a value.
Across rooms: map visuals for routes, the remotes of each room, the age of scouting data, marks on rooms with threats.
A drawing that does not change (a base plan): draw it once, keep the export string in the global scope, and import it on later ticks instead of drawing shape by shape.
Give every kind of visual a switch: a flag in Memory or on global that you set from the console, per room. Drawings for rooms nobody looks at are wasted CPU.
For one value over time use the Memory panel of the client instead of a drawing: mechanic:client-tools.

tasks: show what a creep is doing
draw my base plan in the room
see the state of each creep
pitfalls: A creep shows only its last say() of the tick. Role code and movement code that both speak overwrite each other.
Many icons are two or more characters long for the cut at 10: an icon with text behind it can lose its end.
A dashboard drawn in every room on every tick is paid in every room on every tick. Draw on request, and only the room you watch.
notes: say() shows the first 10 characters for one tick and is free of the intent fee. With true as the second argument other players see the bubble too.
Visuals are text collected during the tick: up to 500 KB per room and 1000 KB for the map. The call that goes over throws.
A drawing call queues no intent. Its cost is the run time of building the text, which grows with every shape.
Visuals are stored for your account under the number of the tick: only you see them, and they must be drawn again every tick.
Community practice: one icon per creep state shows a wrong state at a glance; the wiki keeps a table of icons for actions and structures.
Community practice: room visuals for paths, the status of structures, CPU and whole dashboards; map visuals for scouting, observers and long routes.

intent fee

entries.name: Talk to other players: signs, say, public segments, messages, alliances
entries.title: Talk to other players: signs, say, public segments, messages, alliances
entries.summary: What the game offers for dealing with neighbours: a sign of up to 100 characters on any controller, speech bubbles that others can see, memory segments that the code of another player can read, the message box of the client, and resources sent through terminals. An alliance is an agreement between players and nothing more: to the game every other player is the same.

steps.text: Find out who the neighbour is: the owner and the sign of their rooms (controller.owner.username, controller.sign), what their creeps say in public, their profile in the client.
Say what you intend where they will read it: sign your own controllers and those of the rooms you use (remotes, a room you plan to claim). Any creep next to a controller can sign it.

Write to them. The client has a message box for every player, reached from the profile. For anything that needs a yes from the other side (a border, a remote, passage) a direct message is the first step.
Agree on rules that code can keep: which rooms are whose, which creeps may pass where, what is traded for what.

Teach your code the agreement: a list of friendly user names in Memory, checked wherever the game says hostile: tower targets, defender targets, the trigger of safe mode, the choice of rangedMassAttack.
Passage: open the ramparts on the agreed way with setPublic(true) while no enemy is in the room, and close them when one shows up.
Contact between programs: publish a segment with what others should know (resources you ask for, rooms under attack, your list of friends) and read theirs: recipe:share-data-with-an-ally.
Help: send resources with terminal.send, where the description says what it is for, or join a defence with creeps.
Alliances: groups of players with a shared list of friends, a chat channel and often a common segment format. One joins by asking its members.

tasks: how to talk to another player
leave a message on a controller
let an ally through my ramparts
pitfalls: An agreement that your code does not know is broken by your own towers, since the default target list holds every foreign creep. Put the names in before the ally arrives.
rangedMassAttack damages everything in range that another player owns, allies included. Next to friendly creeps use rangedAttack.
A public rampart lets the creeps of every other player through, friend or not, and covers whoever stands on it.
Your safe mode stops allies as well: while it runs, the creeps of every other player in the room can neither heal nor attack. Helpers are of use before it starts or after it ends.
notes: The game has no status of friend: FIND_HOSTILE_CREEPS returns every creep that is not yours, the creeps of an ally among them.
A sign holds up to 100 characters and shows the name of the signer and the time. Signing needs range 1 and no body part, on any controller; an empty text removes the sign.
What a creep of another player said is in creep.saying only when it was said with public set.
A public segment can be read by every player who knows your name, not only by friends.
The description of a terminal transfer, up to 100 characters, is stored with the transaction and shows in the incoming transactions of the receiver.
Open backend: a message is text of up to 102,400 characters. The addressee finds it in the message box and gets a notification.
The terms of service forbid harassing or threatening material; signs, public say and messages are read by people and fall under them.
Community practice: players reach each other through the messages of the client, controller signs, public say and public segments, and through the community chat outside the game.
Community practice: alliances rest on mutual defence, trade and sometimes shared code. A community site keeps a public register of alliances and their members.

Community practice: an account that runs an open-source bot unchanged is called an NCP (non-coding player). The terms of service allow it, but the wiki reports that many players are hostile to such accounts; say in a sign or a message what you run and what you intend.

entries.name: Plan a base by code: layout, roads, rampart line
entries.title: Plan a base by code: layout, roads, rampart line
entries.summary: Community practice for laying out a room without placing sites by hand: choose a layout style, find where it fits on the terrain, fix the spots at sources and controller, draw roads from stored paths, close the base with a short rampart line, and place the sites level by level. The game sets only the ranges and the counts.

steps.text: Read the terrain once. It needs no vision, so a room can be planned before it is claimed; the positions of sources, mineral and controller need one look into the room.

Choose the style. Bunker: one fixed layout around an anchor tile; least code, needs one large open area. Stamps: small fixed groups (hub, extension clusters, lab block, towers) placed one after another; fit more rooms, more code. Generated: rules and a flood fill grow the layout; fits any room, hardest to get right.
Distance transform: give every tile its distance to the nearest wall tile, counting the two outer rings as wall. A square of odd side s fits around a tile whose value is at least (s + 1) / 2.
Among the tiles where the layout fits, take as anchor the one with the shortest summed paths to the sources, the controller and the mineral.

Fix the outer spots: a miner tile next to each source with a container under it and later a link beside it; tiles for upgraders within range 3 of the controller with a container or link next to them; a container beside the mineral.

Core: storage, terminal, a link, factory and power spawn around one tile, so that one creep standing there serves all of them. Labs so that each is within range 2 of the two source labs. Extensions where a filler passes at range 1. Free tiles next to every spawn.

Roads: search from the storage to each source, the controller, the mineral and the exits in use. Before each search give the tiles already chosen as road a lower cost than plain, so that later paths join earlier ones.

Rampart line: a minimum cut between the exit tiles and the tiles to protect gives the fewest ramparts that close the base. Keep the line 3 tiles away from what it protects, or put ramparts on those structures as well.

Store the plan and place sites from it as each room level allows, most needed first: spawn, extensions, tower, storage, then the rest; roads and ramparts when energy is spare. Check now and then for planned structures that are missing.

tasks: how to plan a base automatically
lay out a room by code
where to put ramparts with minimum cut
distance transform to find space for a base
where to place extensions labs and towers
pitfalls: Roads placed wherever creeps happen to walk spread into webs nobody uses, because paths differ from tick to tick. Community practice: build roads only from stored paths.
At most 100 sites per player over all rooms: place by priority, or road sites in one room hold up a tower in another.
Your own site for a blocking structure stops your own creeps. Do not put a whole level of sites across the paths in use at once.
Only 1 storage and 1 terminal are allowed, and sites count like structures: moving one means destroying it first. Put them where the level 8 plan wants them.
notes: Community practice: the three styles and the three algorithms (distance transform, flood fill, minimum cut) are the common toolkit. The game prescribes none of them.
Ranges that pin the layout: harvest, transfer and withdraw reach 1 tile; build, repair and upgradeController 3; a lab reaction 2; a ranged attack 3.

Level 8 allows 91 structures besides roads, walls, ramparts, containers and the extractor. In a checkerboard of structures and roads that is about 182 tiles, a square of 14 a side: plan for all of it from the start.
Nothing can be built on the border ring, and on the ring next to it only roads and containers. A rampart line at an exit therefore stands 2 tiles inside the room.
A finished creep leaves the spawn onto a free adjacent tile, TOP first unless directions are set. With all eight tiles built over it never comes out.
A tower does 600 damage up to range 5 and 150 from range 20. Community practice differs: towers in one cluster are easy to fill and to cover; towers spread toward the rampart line hit harder there.
A nuke hits the 5 × 5 tiles around its target: 10,000,000 in the middle, 5,000,000 on the others. A tight core loses more to one nuke; a spread one needs more ramparts and longer fill routes.
Every rampart costs 0.01 energy per hit to raise and 0.03 per tick to hold, so what the cut should make small is the number of ramparts (table).

Community practice: the line goes around each exit, around the base by minimum cut, or across choke points of the terrain. Walls in it cost nothing to hold, since they do not decay, but they block your own creeps too.

entries.name: Is this remote source worth mining
entries.title: Is this remote source worth mining
entries.summary: What one source in a room you do not own brings and costs per tick. Reserved it gives 10 energy per tick; miner, hauler, reserver and upkeep come off that, and the hauler alone costs 0.02 per tick for every road tile. Community practice is to rank sources by this net and take the nearest first.

steps.text: Measure d: the length in tiles of the path from the drop-off (storage, or a link near the exit) to the tile next to the source. Use the path the road will be built on.
Income: 10 energy per tick from a reserved source, 5 from an unreserved one.
Miner: 6 WORK, 1 CARRY, 3 MOVE (800 energy). It walks d ticks of its life, so it costs 800 ÷ (1500 − d) per tick.
Hauler: CARRY parts = income × 2 × d ÷ 50, half as many MOVE on a road; cost per tick = body cost ÷ 1500. For a reserved source that is 0.02 energy per tick for every tile of d.
Reserver: 2 CLAIM + 2 MOVE (1300 energy) hold the room for 2 × (600 − d) ticks: 1300 ÷ that per tick, shared by all sources of the room.
Upkeep: container 0.5 per tick, road 0.001 per plain tile per tick plus the wear of the creeps that use it.
Net = income − miner − hauler − reserver − upkeep (table). Take the source when the net is worth the spawn time and the CPU it ties up, and the nearest sources before the far ones.
Then plan for raids and invader cores: a guard on call, or miners that leave the room for a while (recipe:defend-against-invaders).

tasks: is this remote room worth mining
what does remote mining cost per tick
how far away can I mine a remote
is reserving a remote worth the energy
net income of a remote source
how much spawn time does a remote need
pitfalls: A raid is due about every 100,000 energy harvested in the room: every 10,000 ticks for one reserved source. Count the guard, or the creeps lost, into the net.
While an invader core holds the reservation nothing can be harvested and the creeps go on costing.
Without a road a loaded hauler needs one MOVE per CARRY to keep one tile per tick on plain: 100 energy per 50 carried instead of 75, but no road to build or hold.
The container holds 2000, 200 ticks of a reserved source. What a late hauler leaves over lies on the ground and shrinks.
notes: Income: a source refills to 3000 every 300 ticks in a reserved room and to 1500 in an unreserved one.
Miner: 5 WORK empty a reserved source. A tick that repairs cannot harvest, so one more WORK part buys the ticks for keeping the container up.
Hauler: 0.4 CARRY per tile of d for a reserved source. On a road one MOVE moves two loaded CARRY at one tile per tick.

Reserver: every CLAIM part adds 1 tick per tick and 1 tick runs off, so n CLAIM parts working W ticks hold the room for n × W. With one MOVE per CLAIM a reserved tick costs 650 ÷ (600 − walk) energy, whatever n is.

Upkeep: a container in a room without owner loses 5000 hits every 100 ticks, a plain road tile 100 every 1000, at 0.01 energy per hit. Each body part that steps on a road tile brings its next decay 1 tick closer: 0.001 energy.
One-off: 300 energy per plain road tile, 1500 on swamp, 5000 for the container. A 50-tile plain road with a container is 20,000 energy.
Energy is not the only price: every body part takes 3 ticks of a spawn, and every creep at least 0.2 CPU per tick for its one intent.
Community practice: miner and hauler per source, a shared reserver, a guard and a road repairer shared by several rooms; the wiki has its own cost analysis by distance.

entries.name: Choose the next room to claim
entries.title: Choose the next room to claim
entries.summary: Community practice for picking a room to expand into: score the candidates from scouting data by sources, mineral, remote sources around them, distance to your rooms, neighbours and terrain. No rule decides it; the code only sets what a room can give and how far a claimer gets (600 ticks).

steps.text: A free slot: Game.gcl.level above the number of rooms you own. Check the CPU as well: every room adds creeps, and every creep its intents.
Candidates: rooms with a controller (no highway, keeper or centre room) that are open to you, without owner and without a reservation of someone else.
Look into each candidate once, by scout or observer, and store: number and positions of sources, mineral type, owner, reservation and sign of the controller, hostile structures.
Sources: two give 20 energy per tick, one gives 10.
Mineral: prefer a type that none of your rooms has. What is missing for a compound has to be bought or carried in.
Remotes: count the sources in the rooms around it that nobody uses. Each is worth its net in recipe:remote-mining-economics; keeper rooms next door hold sources of 4000.
Distance to your nearest room: near enough for the claimer, for helpers and for defenders; far enough that the two rooms do not want the same remotes (table).
Terrain: your layout must fit (recipe:base-planning); few and narrow exits make a short rampart line; a road tile on swamp costs 5 times one on plain.
Neighbours: owned and reserved rooms around it, who mines where, what the signs say. A room next to an active player needs defence from its first day.
Weigh these as you see fit, take the best candidate, and go on with recipe:claim-a-room.

tasks: which room should I claim next
how to choose a room to expand into
which mineral should my next room have
how far away can I claim a room
one source or two source room
pitfalls: Community practice: do not expand while your rooms are short of CPU or energy or under attack. A new room takes builders, energy and guards from the old ones before it gives anything back.
Community practice: a badly placed room is given up and replaced once the energy allows. unclaim() sets the controller to level 0 with no progress, so the whole climb is paid again.
A room that looked free can be claimed or reserved by the time the claimer arrives: look again before it sets out, and on arrival.
notes: Community practice: the usual criteria are two sources, a mineral you lack, the remote sources around, the distance to your rooms and the players nearby. How to weigh them is each player's choice.
The claim itself needs a GCL level above the rooms you own, and a controller at level 0 that nobody else reserved.
A one-source room earns 10 energy per tick, less than the 15 its controller can take at level 8. A two-source room earns 20.
A room has one mineral: 15,000 to 100,000 units when full, refilled 50,000 ticks after it has been emptied.
Every boost needs H or O, tier 2 and tier 3 need both (as OH), tier 3 needs X on top. Community practice: cover O and H with the first rooms, the others after.
A claimer lives 600 ticks and cannot be renewed: at one tile per tick that is at most 12 rooms of 50 tiles in a straight line, fewer on a real path.
Later the two rooms trade through terminals, and that costs by distance: 96 energy per 1000 units at 3 rooms, 284 at 10.
Raids enter only through exits to rooms that are neither owned nor reserved. A room whose neighbours you hold gets none.

entries.name: Spawn queue: priorities, body size, recovery
entries.title: Spawn queue: priorities, body size, recovery
entries.summary: Community practice for deciding what a spawn makes next: a priority order with the filler first, bodies sized to the energy at hand, replacements ordered before the old creep dies, and a small creep that restarts a room with no creeps left. One spawn keeps at most 500 body parts alive.

steps.text: Count what is alive per job, in body parts rather than heads: WORK parts on each source, CARRY parts on each route. Leave out creeps that are about to die.

Order the needs. A common order: the filler of spawn and extensions, miners, defenders while hostiles are in the room, haulers, then upgraders and builders, then everything that only adds (remotes, mineral, scouts).
Normal size: the largest body of the wanted shape that the room capacity pays, up to what the job needs.
Emergency size: when no filler or no miner is alive, build what the energy at hand pays, down to [WORK, CARRY, MOVE] for 200.
Each tick an idle spawn takes the first need on the list that the room can pay. While the filler is missing, nothing else is taken.
Replace ahead of time: put the successor on the list when ticksToLive falls to 3 × its parts + the walk to its work place.
Decide per job whether to renew instead: it suits creeps that stand next to a spawn anyway and creeps too large for the room to build now.
Watch the budget: sum parts × 3 over everything wanted in 1500 ticks. Above 1500 per spawn, the lowest needs never get built; cut them or wait for the next spawn.

tasks: what should my spawn build next
in which order to spawn creeps
all my creeps died how do I recover
restart a room after a wipe
how big should the next creep be
when to spawn a replacement creep
how many creeps can one spawn support
should I renew creeps or spawn new ones
pitfalls: A list that only knows full-size bodies never recovers: without a filler the room does not reach its capacity again. Community practice calls the small restart creep a cold boot.
Creeps with a CLAIM part live 600 ticks and cannot be renewed: reservers are always spawned anew.
A 50-part creep keeps a spawn busy for 150 ticks. Put the filler and the defenders before it, not behind.
notes: Community practice: bots grow from a fixed head count per role, to counting the body parts each job needs, to a queue that other parts of the code push requests into.
A spawn makes one creep at a time, 3 ticks per part, and a creep lives 1500 ticks: 500 parts per spawn at the very most.
The whole body cost is taken at once from spawns and extensions. Above the first 300 energy only creeps refill them, which is why the filler leads every order.
With no creep left, a spawn still gains 1 energy per tick while the room holds less than 300: a [WORK, CARRY, MOVE] is affordable after 200 ticks at the latest.
Rounding aside, renewing costs the same energy per tick of life as a new creep, and gives 1.2 times the life per tick the spawn is busy.
One renew call needs only its own cost in the room, 0.4 × body cost ÷ parts: a young room can keep alive a creep it could never build.

Community practice, renew against respawn. Renewing keeps the creep and its memory and leaves the spawn free sooner; it strips boosts, takes one intent per call and keeps the creep waiting at the spawn. A new creep is one intent and can be ordered ahead; the spawn is busy for its whole spawn time.

entries.name: Move energy: haulers, fillers, links, terminals
entries.title: Move energy: haulers, fillers, links, terminals
entries.summary: Community practice for moving energy. Haulers are sized from energy per tick × round trip ÷ 50; a filler serves spawn and extensions on a fixed route; from room level 5 links replace the long hauls inside a room, and from level 6 terminals replace creeps between rooms.

steps.text: Measure every route once: the path length from pick-up to drop-off. A round trip is twice that plus the ticks to load and unload.
Size the hauling: CARRY parts = energy per tick × round trip ÷ 50; one MOVE per two CARRY on roads, one per CARRY without (table). Split the parts over as few creeps as the spawn energy allows.

Hand out the work. One hauler per miner is simple and leaves haulers waiting. A pool that always takes the fullest pick-up uses them better, but needs one place that gives out the jobs so that two haulers do not go for the same energy.
Pick-up: from the container under the miner; without one, or when it overflows, pickup from the pile.
Drop-off: spawn and extensions first, towers under a threshold, the rest to storage. From room level 4 haulers deliver to storage only and a filler works from there.

Filler: either a fixed route past all extensions, or creeps that stand between the storage (or a link) and a block of extensions and never walk. Give spawnCreep the same order in opts.energyStructures.
From level 5 links take the long hauls: source link to storage link, storage link to controller link. One source fills a link in 80 ticks.
Between two rooms that both have a terminal, send; creeps carry only to rooms below level 6 (table). Even out stocks as in recipe:balance-resources-between-rooms.

tasks: how many haulers do I need
how many CARRY parts for a hauler
how big should a hauler be
fixed route for the filler creep
one hauler per miner or a hauler pool
pitfalls: The receiving link has to be emptied. When it is full nothing arrives, the source link fills up, and the miner's energy drops on the ground.
Hauling by creep between two rooms with terminals wastes energy: per 1000 delivered a terminal burns 33 at 1 room and 154 at 5, a road hauler's body costs several times that (table).
A container is full after 200 ticks of one source. What comes after that lies on the ground and shrinks, so a pool should send the next free hauler to the fullest container.
notes: Community practice: haulers develop from creeps that fetch whatever they find, to one hauler per miner, to haulers that are given tasks by one manager.
An owned or reserved source needs 0.4 CARRY per tile of one-way distance. A body has 50 parts, so one road hauler (33 CARRY) covers 82 tiles; beyond that it takes two.
An empty CARRY part weighs nothing: a hauler walks out at full speed on any terrain, and only the loaded way back needs the road.

Pile or container: a pile loses ceil(amount ÷ 1000) per tick, so 1 per tick up to 1000. A container loses nothing, holds 2000, and costs 0.1 energy per tick in your room and 0.5 in a room without owner.

A link loses 3% of what it sends: 0.3 energy per tick for one source. A road hauler costs 0.02 per tick per tile, so in energy the link is ahead beyond 15 tiles; it also saves the spawn time and the intents of the hauler.

Community practice for links: roles are source, storage, controller, and a link near an exit for haulers from remote rooms. Send rules are fixed pairs (source to storage), a priority list of receivers, or evening out all links to one level.

By default a spawn pays from the spawns first and then from the extensions nearest to it. Community practice: refill along a fixed route and pass that order as energyStructures, so that what is spent first is refilled first.
A full refill at level 8 is 12,900 energy (200 per extension); at level 6 it is 2300. A filler with n CARRY moves 50 × n per trip.
Every withdraw, transfer and move that succeeds costs 0.2 CPU. Few large haulers are cheaper in CPU than many small ones, and passing energy from creep to creep costs one intent for each hand.

entries.name: Trade on the market: first credits, deal or order, arbitrage
entries.title: Trade on the market: first credits, deal or order, arbitrage
entries.summary: Community practice on the market: earn the first credits by dealing to buy orders, count the transfer energy into every price, deal for dear goods and place orders for cheap bulk and for energy. An order costs 5% of its value up front; a deal costs the dealer the energy.

steps.text: First credits without a terminal (official server): turn a full bucket into a pixel and deal pixels to a buy order.
First credits with a terminal (room level 6): deal spare energy or the mineral of the room to the best buy order. Selling by deal needs no credits.
Read the orders of one resource now and then, not every tick, and keep the result.
Hold each price against avgPrice and stddevPrice of the last days. Leave out orders far off the average.
Count the energy into the price: who deals pays it. A sale by deal brings price × amount minus the transfer energy at what energy is worth to you.

Deal or order. A deal is instant and costs you the energy. An order costs 5% up front, waits, and leaves the energy to the other side. Cheap bulk and energy itself: order. Dear goods in small amounts: deal (table).
An order that does not fill: move its price. Lowering is free, raising costs the fee on the increase only; cancelling and creating again pays the whole fee twice.
Stock rules per resource: a floor you keep, a ceiling above which you sell, a level below which you buy. Sell what your rooms mine too much of and buy the minerals no room of yours has.
Cancel filled orders: they stay in Game.market.orders and count toward the 300.

tasks: how to get my first credits
should I buy energy on the market
how to price a market order
pitfalls: A sale by deal over a long distance can burn more than it earns: at 30 rooms 633 energy per 1000 units sold.
Community practice: read your own orders before creating one, or you bid against yourself and tie up the fee twice.
At most 10 deals per tick and one per terminal per cooldown: a plan that needs many small deals is slower than it looks.
notes: Community practice: the first credits come from dealing to existing buy orders, usually with energy, the mineral of the room or pixels.
Selling to a buy order needs no credits. Only a deal on a sell order is checked against your balance.
The player who deals pays the transfer energy, buying or selling. The owner of the order pays none.
An order costs 5% of price × amount when it is created. Cancelling returns nothing; an order that runs out after 30 days returns the fee of its unfilled part.
At the same price a deal is the cheaper way when one unit is worth more than (1 − e^(−rooms ÷ 30)) ÷ 0.05 units of energy: 5.7 at 10 rooms.

Energy bought by deal arrives short of its own transfer: at 10 rooms 284 of every 1000 are burnt, so it costs 1.4 times the listed price. Community practice: buy energy with a buy order and let the sellers pay the transfer.
The game fixes no price. getHistory gives the average and the deviation per resource and day for the last 14 days.
Raising the price of an order costs the fee on the increase × the remaining amount; lowering it costs nothing.

Community practice, arbitrage: buy from a low sell order and deal to a higher buy order, also between shards by carrying goods through portals. It pays only when the spread covers the energy of both transfers, and every deal blocks the terminal for 10 ticks.

entries.name: A room kept for GCL: temple, praise room
entries.title: A room kept for GCL: temple, praise room
entries.summary: Community practice: one room below level 8 takes the spare energy of the others and turns it into GCL, because the limit of 15 energy per tick exists only on a level 8 controller. It costs a room slot and a steady stream of energy from outside.

steps.text: See whether it pays: add up what your level 8 rooms earn above the 15 per tick each controller takes. Only that surplus feeds such a room.
Choose the room: next to a strong room of yours, with many free tiles within range 3 of the controller and room for storage and terminal beside them.
Feed it: haulers from the neighbour room first, the terminal from room level 6 on, filled by every room with a surplus.
Upgraders: mostly WORK, 1 energy per WORK part per tick, standing still next to the store they draw from. They are built in the neighbour room while this room is small.
Boost them once labs stand: XGH2O turns each energy into 2 points, for 30 compound per WORK part.
At level 8 the limit applies here too. Either keep it as a normal room and choose another, or start it over (next step).
Starting over: unclaim, claim again, and climb from level 1. The buildings stay but switch on again only as the levels return, so energy comes by creep until level 6.

tasks: is a room only for upgrading worth it
how many ticks to the next GCL level
what to do with spare energy when all rooms are level 8
pitfalls: The room takes one of your GCL slots. A normal room in that slot would earn energy and a mineral; this one only spends.
A new level needs a full downgrade timer, and after each level-up the timer starts at half. Points above the requirement are kept meanwhile, so nothing is lost while it fills.
Do not renew boosted upgraders: renewing removes the boost. Community practice is to unboost them shortly before they die, which gives back 15 of the 30 compound per part.
An upgrader with W WORK parts burns W × 1500 energy in its life: 30 WORK parts use up the whole output of 3 sources.
notes: The limit of 15 energy per tick is applied only when the controller is at level 8. Below that every WORK part spends 1 energy per tick, and every point counts for GCL at any level.
With all rooms at level 8, GCL grows by 15 points per room per tick, 30 with XGH2O, whatever lies in the storages (second table). Only PWR_OPERATE_CONTROLLER lifts the limit, for as long as it lasts.
Community practice ("temple", "praising"): one room is kept for upgrading alone and fed by the others.
Upgrading works within range 3 of the controller: 48 tiles at most, fewer where walls are. Those tiles and the energy brought in set the rate.
Boosts multiply the points, not the energy: GH ×1.5, GH2O ×1.8, XGH2O ×2, for 30 compound and 20 energy per WORK part of each creep.
Levels 1 to 8 take 16,380,200 energy in all. The terminal works from level 6, 1,800,200 energy after the claim.

unclaim() sets the controller to level 0 with progress 0, empties the stock of safe modes and, outside a novice area, starts the safe mode cooldown of 50,000 ticks. Structures above the allowance of a level do not work until that level is back.

Community practice at level 8: the room is unclaimed and claimed again, to start over at level 1, at the price of the early levels without terminal, towers or safe mode. The other choice is to keep it as a normal room.

entries.name: What to automate next: from the first spawn to a mature empire
entries.title: What to automate next: from the first spawn to a mature empire
entries.summary: An ordered list of what a bot has to do without its owner, from the first spawn to many level 8 rooms; each step names the entry that explains it. Community practice sets the order: income and spawning first, then defence, expansion, minerals and trade, and last the level 8 work.

steps.text: Room level 1 and 2: workers that harvest, fill the spawn and upgrade with no order given by hand.
Spawning by priority, with a way back from zero creeps. Everything after this depends on it.
From level 2 (550 spawn energy): one miner per source and haulers, so that all 10 energy per tick of each source is taken.
Level 3: the tower, always filled, answers raids (recipe:defend-against-invaders); safe mode stays the last resort (recipe:safe-mode).
Sites placed by code at every new level: extensions, roads, containers, later ramparts (recipe:roads-and-upkeep).
Levels 3 and 4: mine the rooms next door, reserve them, guard them (recipe:reserve-and-remote-mine).
Level 4: the storage as the hub. Level 5: links instead of long hauls (recipe:link-network).
GCL 2: choose and claim a second room (recipe:claim-a-room), and run every room from the same code.
Ramparts over what must survive, raised with spare energy (recipe:keep-ramparts-up), and a defence that answers players, not only invaders.
Before the CPU runs short: stored paths, cached lookups, fewer and larger creeps (recipe:cache-between-ticks, recipe:measure-cpu, recipe:travel-across-rooms).
Level 6: extractor, terminal, labs. Mine the mineral, trade (recipe:market-strategy), even out stocks between rooms (recipe:balance-resources-between-rooms).
Reactions run by code up to tier 3, and boosting as a part of spawning (recipe:labs-and-boosts).
Stored knowledge of the rooms around: free rooms, targets, threats. Scouts first, the observer at level 8.
Keeper rooms, then the highways: deposits and power banks (recipe:harvest-deposits, recipe:observer-and-power), and the factory at level 7 (recipe:factory-production).
Level 8: the upgrade limit, power processing and power creeps (recipe:power, recipe:operator-routine), spare energy into GCL (recipe:gcl-farming).
Offence when the economy carries it: sieges and strongholds (recipe:clear-a-stronghold).

tasks: what to do after the tutorial

how long does each room level take
pitfalls: Remotes before a tower and a guard lose more creeps than they pay for: raids follow the energy harvested, in remote rooms as at home.

Community practice: make each step run without you before the next. A raid that kills every creep breaks spawning code with fixed assumptions, and a room that cannot restart by itself undoes all that was built on top.
notes: Community practice: the order follows the hurdles most bots meet. The wiki lists them, and describes for each system the stages from done by hand to fully automatic.
From level 2 a single miner of 5 WORK and 1 MOVE (550 energy) empties a source; at level 1 a creep with one MOVE holds 2 WORK at most.
Level 3 costs 45,000 energy and every level after it 3 times the one before, up to 10,935,000 for level 8. From level 5 on the pace is set by income, not by what the room may build (table).
GCL 2 needs 1,000,000 upgrade points in all, and the points are the same energy that raises the room: the second room comes while the first climbs from level 5 to 6, sooner with remote income.
Community practice: write for many rooms before the second one. Loop over your rooms and give every creep a home room; code that assumes one room is the usual reason a new room stalls.
Community practice on the official server: turn a full bucket into pixels from the first day. They are the first thing you can sell.
