"Ticks to the next level": the whole income of two sources put into the controller; at level 8 the controller takes 15 per tick. Remote: the net of recipe:remote-mining-economics, reserved as soon as the room can pay its miner (800) and a 1 CLAIM + 1 MOVE creep (650). Roads, containers, walls and ramparts are left out of the last column.

entries.name: The official tutorial bot, section by section
entries.title: The official tutorial bot, section by section
entries.summary: The five tutorial sections build one small bot: a harvester, an upgrader, a builder with extensions, automatic respawning, and a tower. This lists what each section adds and which calls it uses.

steps.text: Section 1, a harvester. The main module exports a loop function; each tick it runs one role function for every creep in Game.creeps.
While the creep has free capacity it harvests the first source that room.find(FIND_SOURCES) returns.
Every action follows one pattern: call it, and when it returns ERR_NOT_IN_RANGE call moveTo with the same target.
When full, the creep transfers its energy to the spawn, which is taken by name from Game.spawns.
Section 2, an upgrader. Each creep has a role name in its memory, and the loop picks the role function by it.
The upgrader harvests while it holds no energy, and otherwise upgrades room.controller.
Section 3, a builder and extensions. The loop also logs energyAvailable of every room in Game.rooms.
The builder keeps a flag in its memory: building once it is full, harvesting again once it is empty. It builds the first site of room.find(FIND_CONSTRUCTION_SITES).
It says a word when it switches, and moveTo gets visualizePathStyle to draw the path.
The harvester now fills every spawn and extension with free energy capacity, found by room.find(FIND_STRUCTURES) with a filter.
Section 4, automatic spawning. The loop first deletes the Memory.creeps entries of creeps that are gone.
It counts the creeps with the role harvester. Below 2 it spawns [WORK, CARRY, MOVE] with a name made from Game.time and the role in opts.memory.
While spawn.spawning is set, it writes the role of the new creep next to the spawn.
Section 5, a tower. The harvester fills towers as well.
The tower is fetched by its id, which you paste into the code.
It repairs the closest structure with hits below hitsMax, found by pos.findClosestByRange with a filter.
It attacks the closest hostile creep.

tasks: which calls does the tutorial use
pitfalls: Section 5 calls tower.repair and tower.attack in the same tick. A tower does one action per tick and repair goes before attack, so while anything in the room is damaged the tower does not shoot. Attack first and repair only when no hostile is there.
The harvest pattern stalls at an empty source: harvest returns ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_RESOURCES before it checks the range, so the creep does not walk there.
Every role takes the first source of the list, so all creeps go to one source.
Game.spawns is keyed by spawn name. The code asks for "Spawn1" and breaks when your spawn has another name.
Section 4 respawns harvesters only. Upgraders and builders need the same count and spawn step.

The engine treats objects marked as tutorial differently: creeps of such a spawn do not age, a level 1 controller needs 4 energy for level 2, and the spawn does not refill itself. Numbers seen in the tutorial need not hold in the world.
facts: Section 1: the loop over Game.creeps, and a harvester that harvests, moves on ERR_NOT_IN_RANGE and transfers to the spawn.

Section 2: roles chosen by creep.memory.role, and an upgrader that calls upgradeController. Its harvester still reads spawn.energy and energyCapacity, which the reference marks as deprecated; later sections use store.
Section 3: a builder with a two-state flag in memory, say on each switch, and a harvester that looks for spawns and extensions with free energy capacity.
Section 4: memory clean-up, a count of harvesters, spawnCreep when there are fewer than 2, and a text next to the spawn while it works.
Section 5: a tower that repairs the closest damaged structure and attacks the closest hostile creep; the harvester also fills towers.
A creep being spawned is already in Game.creeps, which is why section 4 can read its memory while the spawn works.

entries.name: Why does it not work: symptoms and their reasons
entries.title: Why does it not work: symptoms and their reasons
entries.summary: 30 things that go wrong for nearly every player, each with what you see, the reason in the engine, and what to do. The fact with the same number names the code that proves the reason.

steps.text: A call that worked is treated as failed, or `if (creep.harvest(source))` runs on errors: OK is 0 and every error is a negative number. Compare with the constant, `== OK` or `== ERR_NOT_IN_RANGE`.
console.log(object) prints [object Object]: the console joins the text form of each argument. Log JSON.stringify(object) instead.
A fill check never fires because store.getFreeCapacity() is null: on a spawn, extension, tower, link or lab the capacity methods need the resource. Write getFreeCapacity(RESOURCE_ENERGY).

Creeps stand still instead of walking to a source: at an empty source harvest returns ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_RESOURCES before it checks the range, so the test for ERR_NOT_IN_RANGE never fires. build, repair and upgradeController do the same when the creep has no energy. Decide to move by distance.
A creep does not move: moveTo returned ERR_TIRED (fatigue above 0) or ERR_NO_BODYPART (no MOVE part with hits left). Add MOVE parts or roads, or heal it.

A creep pushes against a blocked tile for several ticks: moveTo keeps its path in creep.memory._move and follows it for reusePath ticks (5 unless you set it) without searching again. Lower reusePath where traffic is dense.

A PathFinder.search path runs through structures or creeps: the search knows terrain only. Return a CostMatrix from roomCallback with 255 on blocked tiles. Room.findPath and moveTo build that matrix themselves.

A path kept in Memory stops working (ERR_NOT_FOUND): Memory is JSON, so positions come back as plain objects, and moveByPath then expects findPath steps with dx, dy and direction. Store the string from Room.serializePath, or rebuild RoomPosition objects.

A creep flips between two rooms every tick: a creep standing on an exit tile is sent to the next room each tick it stands there. Never end a move on a tile with x or y of 0 or 49; aim at a tile further inside.

A structure blinks red and its methods return ERR_RCL_NOT_ENOUGH: it is inactive, the room level allows fewer of its type. Those nearest the controller stay active; remove the others or raise the level. A wall with 1 hit also blinks red: repair it.

repair returns OK but a wall or rampart gains nothing: its hitsMax is 0. In a room with a controller, walls can be repaired from room level 2, and a rampart only in a room owned by the rampart's owner.

Controller progress is past progressTotal but the level does not rise: the level only goes up while the downgrade timer is within 100 ticks of its maximum. Keep upgrading; every tick with an upgrade adds 100 to the timer.
room.energyAvailable is less than what the spawns and extensions hold: inactive ones are left out, and spawning cannot use their energy either.
spawnCreep returns ERR_INVALID_ARGS: the body must be one flat array of 1 to 50 part constants (an array inside the array fails), and the name is required.

spawnCreep returned OK but nothing is spawning: two spawns of one room were started in the same tick. Both passed the energy check of the start of the tick, and the second found too little left. Start one per room and tick, or give each its own energyStructures.

A new creep starts with the memory of a dead one, and Memory.creeps keeps growing: spawnCreep without opts.memory keeps what is stored under that name. Delete the entries of names that are no longer in Game.creeps, as the tutorial does.
A finished creep stays inside the spawn: every tile in the allowed directions is blocked, and the spawn tries again each tick. Keep a tile free, or allow more directions with spawning.setDirections.
A tower repairs but never shoots: a tower does one action per tick, heal before repair before attack. Call only the action you want this tick.

A creep action returned OK and did not happen: of heal, rangedHeal, attackController, dismantle, repair, build, attack and harvest only the first one in this order runs in a tick. Call one of them per tick.
dismantle on an invader core returns ERR_INVALID_TARGET: dismantle only works on structure types that can be built. Use attack or rangedAttack.
rangedMassAttack does no damage to roads, containers or walls: it only hits objects that have an owner other than you, and power banks. Use rangedAttack, attack or dismantle on those.

attack, dismantle or heal returns ERR_NO_BODYPART although the creep has the part: either the room is in another player's safe mode, or the part has 0 hits left. Damage takes parts from the front of the body.
build returns ERR_INVALID_TARGET on a good site: a creep stands on the site of a structure that blocks movement. Move the creep away. Roads, containers and ramparts can be built under creeps.

createConstructionSite returns ERR_RCL_NOT_ENOUGH although you have fewer than allowed: every structure and site of that type in the room counts, those of a previous owner too. Destroy the leftovers first.
transfer returns ERR_FULL although the target has room: with an explicit amount the whole amount has to fit. Leave the amount out to send what fits.
transfer into a lab returns ERR_INVALID_TARGET: the lab still holds another mineral. A lab takes energy and one other resource; empty it before you change the mineral.

Game.getObjectById returns null, or Game.rooms[name] is undefined, for something that exists: you have no vision of that room. A room is visible only while one of your objects (not a flag or a construction site) is in it, or while an observer watches it.
Memory is null: the stored string is not valid JSON, for example after RawMemory.set with broken text. Write valid JSON with RawMemory.set to get it back.

The intents and Memory changes of a tick are lost and the console shows a memory segment error: a segment over 100 KB, a segment that is not a string, or more than 10 entries in RawMemory.segments makes the runtime throw after your code. Check the length before you assign.

The console shows "Script execution has been terminated: CPU bucket is empty" and your code did not run: the bucket is below 0, so the tick is skipped and the bucket gets one tick of your limit back. Stay under your limit until it has recovered.

tasks: why does my code not work
why is my structure blinking red
creep blinking between two rooms at an exit
why does the controller not level up
creep keeps the memory of a dead creep
a call returns OK but nothing happens
pitfalls: A return code is checked against the state at the start of the tick. OK means the call was accepted, not that it will happen: another creep can empty the store or fill the target first.
facts: 1. OK is 0 and the error codes run from -1 to -16. ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_ENERGY, ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_RESOURCES and ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_EXTENSIONS are the same number, -6.
2. console.log turns every argument into text with toString() and joins them with spaces.
3. Without a resource, the capacity methods return null on a store that has per-resource capacities.
4. harvest checks the source's energy before the range; build, repair and upgradeController check the creep's energy before the range.
5. moveTo returns ERR_TIRED while fatigue is above 0 and ERR_NO_BODYPART without a working MOVE part.
6. moveTo stores the path under creep.memory._move and reuses it until reusePath ticks have passed; the default is 5.
7. PathFinder.search gets terrain plus whatever roomCallback returns; Room.findPath marks obstacles in its own cost matrix.
8. moveByPath treats an array as positions only if its first element is a RoomPosition; otherwise it looks for steps with dx and dy. Memory is written with JSON.stringify.
9. Every tick a player creep is on an edge tile, it is handed over to the neighbouring room.

10. The room renderer draws a blinking red square over an object flagged as disabled, and over a wall with 1 hit. In the engine a structure is disabled when the room level does not cover it, counted from the controller outwards.
11. Walls get hitsMax 0 where the room level allows no walls, ramparts where the room is not their owner's; repair skips a target without hitsMax.
12. The level-up needs enough progress and a downgrade timer at most 100 ticks below the maximum of the current level.
13. energyAvailable adds up spawns and extensions that are not switched off, and so does the spawn when it pays for a creep.
14. Each body element must itself be a part constant, the length must be 1 to 50, and a missing name is refused.
15. The script-side check uses the room's energy at the start of the tick; when the intent is processed the spawn gives up if the energy is no longer there.
16. spawnCreep writes opts.memory to Memory.creeps[name], and without it keeps the entry that is already there. The tutorial loop removes entries of creeps that are gone.
17. When no allowed neighbouring tile is free the creep is not placed and the spawn time is moved one tick on.
18. Of the tower intents of a tick only one runs: heal, else repair, else attack.
19. Each of these actions is dropped when one that ranks above it was called in the same tick.
20. dismantle refuses every target type without a construction cost; an invader core has none.
21. The mass attack picks targets that have an owner field and are not yours, plus power banks. Roads, containers and built walls have no owner.
22. The same code, ERR_NO_BODYPART, is returned for a missing working part and for a room in someone else's safe mode. A part counts only while it has hits.
23. A site for a structure that blocks movement cannot be built while a creep is on its tile.
24. The count for the room level takes all structures and sites of the type in the room, without looking at the owner.
25. With an amount, transfer returns ERR_FULL when amount plus what is stored is above the capacity.
26. Once a lab holds a mineral it has capacity for energy and that mineral only, and transfer refuses a resource without capacity.
27. Your script gets the rooms that hold one of your objects (flags and construction sites do not count) and the rooms your observers watch. getObjectById only knows objects of those rooms.
28. When the stored Memory string cannot be parsed, the Memory object is null for that tick.
29. The segment checks run after your loop and throw; the result of the run, intents and Memory included, is then never saved.
30. With a bucket below 0 the script is not started that tick; the bucket is raised by the CPU limit instead.

entries.name: Save CPU: what costs and the cheaper way
entries.title: Save CPU: what costs and the cheaper way
entries.summary: A checklist of where CPU goes: intents at 0.2 each, path searches, parsing Memory, repeated finds, and work done every tick without need. With the cheaper way for each.

steps.text: Measure first: wrap the large blocks (per room, per role) and log the sums. See recipe:measure-cpu.

Intents: every call that returns OK costs 0.2. Skip calls that change nothing (repair at full hits, upgrade without energy) and test range yourself before calling. One move plus one work action per creep is 0.4 per tick.
Movement: raise reusePath (default 5) for creeps on fixed routes, pass ignoreCreeps on long trips, and for routes walked all day store the path once and follow it with moveByPath.
Path searches: give range 1 or more for goals nobody can stand on, keep maxOps low for near targets, and keep cost matrices in the global scope instead of building them per search.
Finds: call find once per room and tick, filter once, hand the list to every creep. Take findClosestByRange unless walls between you and the target matter.
Targets: store the id and look it up. Do not search every tick for the same source, container or controller.
Memory: keep it small. It is parsed on the first touch of every tick and written back after the loop. Bulky data goes to a segment, data you can recompute goes to the global scope.
Spread work: run planning, market checks and repair target lists every N ticks (Game.time % N), with a different offset per room so they do not land on the same tick.
Use the bucket as a switch: skip optional work when it is low, run the heavy jobs when it is full.
Looking: lookForAt for the one kind you need instead of lookAt; read terrain in loops through Room.getTerrain().get.
Fewer, larger creeps: each creep costs its intents and its logic every tick, whatever its size.

tasks: why is my cpu so high
pitfalls: moveTo that cannot use its stored path runs a full search in that tick. A creep stuck behind another one can do that every tick.
moveTo across rooms searches again in every room it enters, each time with up to 20000 ops.
creep.memory, room.memory and flag.memory all read Memory and so trigger the parse; so does moveTo with its stored path.
The Memory save after the loop is charged but is not in any Game.cpu.getUsed() reading: a large Memory costs more than a profile shows.
Every tick is booked as at least 1 CPU, because the amount is rounded up.
notes: The same method called twice on one object in a tick is charged once; say and pull cost nothing.
A call that returns an error code queues nothing and pays no fee, only its own run time.
Room.find without a filter only copies a list made at the start of the tick; the filter is the part that costs on every call.

entries.name: Cache data between ticks
entries.title: Cache data between ticks
entries.summary: Three stores with different costs: the global scope (free, lost on every reset), Memory (kept, but parsed every tick) and segments (kept, 100 KB each, loaded on request). Cache in global; put into Memory only what must survive a reset.

steps.text: Keep ids, not objects. A game object from the last tick is stale; store obj.id and look it up each tick.
Per-tick cache: a result needed many times in one tick (a filtered find) goes into a plain object that you empty when Game.time changes.
Global cache: put long-lived derived data on global or in a module-level variable: cost matrices, room plans, routes. Always write the rebuild: when the entry is missing, compute it again.
What is expensive to rebuild can be saved as well: serialize a cost matrix (625 numbers) into Memory or a segment and deserialize it into global after a reset.
Paths: store them as the serialized string; Creep.moveByPath accepts the string as it is.
Large or seldom needed data: write it into a segment and request the segment one tick before you read it.
Notice a reset: set a module-level variable when the code loads (for example the tick). When it is unset or new, the global scope started empty.

Optional, saves the Memory parse: keep the parsed Memory object in a global variable and at the top of the loop put it back: delete global.Memory; global.Memory = saved; RawMemory._parsed = saved. Use the normal Memory in the first tick after a reset.

tasks: where to keep a cost matrix
pitfalls: A game object put into Memory is saved as a snapshot of its properties. Next tick the action methods reject it; store the id.
A RoomPosition in Memory comes back as plain {x, y, roomName} without methods.
With the parse-skipping step the stored string is never read again while the global lives. Anything that changed Memory outside your loop is overwritten by your copy.
Prototype extensions survive between ticks like any global, and are lost in the same resets. Define them at module level, not inside the loop.
notes: Module-level variables and properties of global live as long as your isolate: until new code is uploaded, the heap overflows, Game.cpu.halt() is called, the script did not run for 3 minutes, or the server restarts.
Code at the top of a module runs once per reset, not once per tick. That is the place to set up caches.
The parse-skipping step works because Memory is a configurable property of global and because the runtime writes back whatever RawMemory._parsed holds after the loop.

entries.name: Travel across rooms
entries.title: Travel across rooms
entries.summary: Send a creep to a room several rooms away: plan the list of rooms with Game.map.findRoute, search the path with PathFinder.search limited to those rooms, and steer by position, because the target room is not visible on the way.

steps.text: Aim at a position: new RoomPosition(25, 25, roomName) works for a room you cannot see. Do not touch Game.rooms[target] on the way.
One or two rooms away: creep.moveTo(pos, {reusePath: 20}) is enough. It searches up to 16 rooms with 20000 ops and plans again in each room it enters.

Further away: get the list of rooms once, with a routeCallback that returns Infinity for rooms to stay out of and a lower cost for highways and your own rooms. Keep the room names in the creep memory.
Search with a roomCallback that returns false for every room not on the route, maxRooms at least the number of rooms on it (limit 64) and a larger maxOps. Give the goal a range.
Follow the stored path with moveByPath; search again when it returns ERR_NOT_FOUND.
On arrival step off the exit tile at once: move at least one tile into the room before doing anything else.
Before sending: check the status of the target room. "closed" means the room is not available; "novice" and "respawn" mark start areas with their own entry rules.

tasks: move a creep to another room
creep stuck on the room border
pitfalls: A creep that ends a tick on an exit tile is moved to the neighbouring room. One that arrives and stays on the exit tile goes straight back.
In rooms without vision the path search knows only terrain. Walls and ramparts built there are found when a creep of yours sees the room.
findRoute returns the number ERR_NO_PATH when there is no route, and looks no further than 30 rooms from the start.
An incomplete search still returns a path. Check incomplete before storing it.
notes: moveTo keeps its path only for the room the creep is in and drops it when the creep enters the next one.
findPath and moveTo return steps up to the exit of the current room only.
The docs show the same plan: findRoute for the rooms, then PathFinder.search with a roomCallback that refuses all other rooms.

entries.name: Measure CPU use
entries.title: Measure CPU use
entries.summary: Find out where the CPU goes: read Game.cpu.getUsed() before and after a block, add up per role or room over many ticks, and judge by the trend of the bucket rather than by single ticks.

steps.text: const t = Game.cpu.getUsed(); run the block; add Game.cpu.getUsed() - t to a counter for that block. The difference contains 0.2 for every intent the block queued.
Take a reading in the first line of the loop. After a reset it shows what loading your modules cost; in other ticks it is near 0.
Measure the Memory parse by itself: one reading before and one after the first touch of Memory in the tick.
Add up: keep sums and counts per role, room or function in the global scope and print the averages every 100 ticks. Single ticks vary too much.
Watch the bucket over time. A falling bucket means the average tick costs more than your limit, whatever the profile says.
Look at the heap too: total_heap_size plus externally_allocated_size close to heap_size_limit means a reset is near.
For a quick profile wrap a prototype method: replace it by a function that takes a reading, calls the original and adds the difference to a counter. Remove the wrapper afterwards.

tasks: how much cpu does a function use
find what uses the most cpu
pitfalls: Writing Memory back (JSON.stringify) happens after the loop and is charged, but no reading inside the loop can show it. Time JSON.stringify(Memory) once to know its size.
The first tick after a global reset compiles and loads every module. Leave it out of the averages.
Console commands run after your loop in the same tick and their CPU is yours as well.
notes: getUsed() is the CPU time of your isolate since the loop was called, plus 0.2 for every intent queued so far.
What the bucket is charged for a tick: run time plus 0.2 per intent, rounded up to a whole number.
In the simulation room getUsed() always returns 0.

entries.name: Share data with an ally: public and foreign segments
entries.title: Share data with an ally: public and foreign segments
entries.summary: One player writes a memory segment and marks it public; the other requests it by user name and reads it one tick later. One foreign segment can be loaded per tick, up to 100 KB.

steps.text: Sender: write a string into a segment with an id from 1 to 99, for example RawMemory.segments[id] = JSON.stringify(data). At most 100 KB.
Sender: put the id on the public list. One call is enough; the list stays until you change it.
Sender, optional: make it the default, so that readers need not know the id.
Reader: request it with the user name of the sender and the id. The request stays active on the following ticks.
Reader, from the next tick: check that foreignSegment exists and that username and id are the ones you asked for, then JSON.parse(data) inside try/catch.
Several allies: only one foreign segment per tick, so go through the list, one ally per tick.
Both directions: each side publishes its own segment and reads the other one. Put the tick number into the data, so the reader can tell new from old.

tasks: read the segment of another player
send a message to the code of another player
pitfalls: Do not publish segment 0: the loader skips an id of 0 and readers never get it.
The reader gets data only while the id is on the public list of the owner. Otherwise foreignSegment is undefined.
A public segment can be read by every player who knows your name. Put nothing in it that an enemy should not see.
setPublicSegments([]) does not take anything back in the public driver. Publish another id, or blank the content.
A segment over 100 KB fails the whole tick of the sender, intents included. Check the length before assigning.
notes: The sender needs no active request to write: every id assigned in RawMemory.segments is saved, up to 10 per tick.
The reader gets what the owner saved at the end of an earlier tick. Count on at least one tick of delay in each direction.
For data between your own shards use InterShardMemory instead.

entries.name: Install a private server, start it and connect
entries.title: Install a private server, start it and connect
entries.summary: Install the `screeps` npm package into an empty folder, run `npx screeps init` once and `npx screeps start` every time. Players connect with the Steam client to port 21025.

steps.text: Have Node.js 22 or newer, npm, Python 3 and a C++ build toolchain on the machine.
In an empty folder: `npm install screeps`. The install compiles native modules and bundles the driver.
`npx screeps init`: enter the Steam Web API key when asked. The folder now holds `.screepsrc`, `db.json`, `mods.json`, `assets` and the example mods.
`npx screeps start`: the launcher prints the version, the game port and the CLI port and starts the processes. Logs go to `logs/`.
In the Steam client choose "Change server" and enter the host, port 21025 and, when one is set, the server password.
In a second terminal `npx screeps cli` opens the admin console.
To keep it running, start it from a service manager with the server folder as working directory.

tasks: set up my own screeps server
what does a private server need
run the server as a service
pitfalls: The contributed Ubuntu guide installs Node 8. The current package needs Node 22: take versions from the README, the service file from the guide.
Without a Steam Web API key and without a Steam client on the machine the backend does not start and nobody can sign in.
Run `start` from the server folder. Elsewhere the launcher finds no `.screepsrc`, warns, and fails for lack of options.
Players need to reach the game port; nobody else should reach the CLI port. The stock file binds the game to all addresses and the CLI to `localhost`.
facts: The package asks for Node.js `>=22.9.0` and npm `>=10.8.2`.
Python 3 and the node-gyp build tools are needed because the install builds native code; after it, a script bundles the driver with webpack.
The three commands are `npm install screeps`, `npx screeps init`, `npx screeps start`.
`init` copies the default files into the folder and writes the Steam key into `.screepsrc`. It stops when the folder already has a `.screepsrc`.
`init` also writes a small `package.json` (name `my-screeps-world`), so mods can be installed into the folder with npm.
`screeps init <dir>` takes a folder; `screeps start` always works in the current directory.
`start` prints the two ports and one line for each started process.
Players connect with the Steam game client: "Change server", then the server address.
Opening the game port in a browser only shows a line that the server is running; it is not a client.
The Steam version of the game comes with a GUI launcher that shows the logs of all processes and the CLI.
As a service: the contributed guide uses a systemd unit that runs `node_modules/screeps/bin/screeps.js start` as its own user, with the server folder as working directory.

entries.name: Change users, rooms and objects from the server CLI
entries.title: Change users, rooms and objects from the server CLI
entries.summary: Direct database commands for an administrator: find a user, set CPU, GCL, credits or power, change a controller, fill a store, finish construction sites, add a terminal or a portal. Each is one line in the server CLI.

steps.text: Open the CLI with `npx screeps cli`.
Find the document. A user: `storage.db.users.findOne({username: "Name"})`. Objects: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].find({room: "W1N1", type: "controller"})`. Note the `_id`.
Change it with `update(query, {$set: {field: value}})` and read the answer: `{ modified: 1 }` means one document changed.
Add an object with `insert({type, room, x, y, …})`, remove one with `removeWhere({_id: "<id>"})`.
Look at the room in the client. The engine picks the change up on its next tick for that room.

tasks: set the gcl of a user
set the room level from the cli
fill a storage with energy on my server
read the memory of a user
add a portal or an npc terminal
pitfalls: `find` returns copies. Changing a returned object in the prompt changes nothing: write with `update`, `insert` or `removeWhere`.
`removeWhere` deletes every document that matches, at once and for good; with `{}` that is the whole collection. Run the same query with `count` first.
An `update` whose query matches nothing answers `{}` and changes nothing. A typo in a room or user name looks like success unless you read the answer.
The database stores whatever you write: nothing checks a hand-made document against what the engine expects. Copy `db.json` before larger edits.
Raising a room level builds nothing. It only allows more structures; sites and structures still have to be placed and built.
The game constants are not available in the prompt. Numbers such as hits or capacities must be typed.
facts: `storage.db.users.findOne({username: "Name"})` shows a user document. Its `_id` is the user id that objects, code and memory refer to.
CPU: `storage.db.users.update({username: "Name"}, {$set: {cpu: 300}})`. The script sees it as `Game.cpu.limit` from its next run. One tick can still use no more than `cpuMaxPerTick`, 500.
GCL: the field `gcl` holds points, not the level. Level N needs 1000000 × (N − 1)^2.4 points; for level 5: `storage.db.users.update({username: "Name"}, {$set: {gcl: 1000000 * Math.pow(4, 2.4)}})`.
Credits: the field `money` counts thousandths of a credit. `{$set: {money: 1000000}}` gives 1000 credits.
Power level: the field `power` holds processed power. Level N needs 1000 × N^2.
A script runs only while the user's `active` is not 0 and `cpu` is above 0. `{$set: {cpu: 0}}` stops a user's code; it also blocks placing a spawn.
`{$set: {blocked: true}}` on a user refuses the placing of a first spawn.
Memory: `storage.env.get(storage.env.keys.MEMORY + "<user id>")` returns the player's Memory as a JSON string. A segment: `storage.env.hget(storage.env.keys.MEMORY_SEGMENTS + "<user id>", 0)`.
The current tick: `storage.env.get(storage.env.keys.GAMETIME)`.

Objects of a room: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].find({room: "W1N1", type: "creep"})`. Types seen in the code include `controller`, `source`, `mineral`, `spawn`, `creep`, `constructionSite`, `terminal`, `powerBank`, `deposit`, `portal`, `invaderCore`.

Room level: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].update({room: "W1N1", type: "controller"}, {$set: {level: 8, progress: 0, downgradeTime: null}})`. With `downgradeTime` empty the engine starts a full downgrade timer on its next tick.
Safe mode fields of a controller: `safeModeAvailable` (how many are left), `safeMode` (the tick it ends), `safeModeCooldown` (the tick the cooldown ends).
Fill a store: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].update({_id: "<id>"}, {$set: {store: {energy: 500000}}})`. `$set` replaces the whole store; `{$merge: {store: {energy: 500000}}}` keeps the other resources.

Construction sites: a site becomes a structure only through a build action, so set `progress` just below `progressTotal` and let a creep do the last point: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].find({type: "constructionSite", room: "W1N1"}).then(l => l.forEach(s => storage.db["rooms.objects"].update({_id: s._id}, {$set: {progress: s.progressTotal - 1}})))`.
Life of a creep: `ageTime` is the tick at which it dies. `storage.db["rooms.objects"].update({_id: "<id>"}, {$set: {ageTime: 5000000}})` lets it live until tick 5,000,000.
Remove an object: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].removeWhere({_id: "<id>"})`.

NPC terminal: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].insert({type: "terminal", room: "W0N0", x: 25, y: 25, store: {}})`. A terminal without `user` gets NPC market orders from the next run of the order job. Give it a `store`, because scripts that look at it read that field.

Portal: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].insert({type: "portal", room: "W5N5", x: 25, y: 25, destination: {room: "W1N8", x: 25, y: 25}})`. A creep that stands on it is moved to the destination. It works one way; insert a second one for the way back.
A portal without `decayTime` and `unstableDate` stays for good. `decayTime` is the tick it vanishes; `unstableDate` is a time in milliseconds after which a decay of 30,000 ticks starts.

A room without player objects is processed only when something wakes it; the server wakes every open room about every 100 ticks. To have an inserted object tick at once: `storage.env.sadd(storage.env.keys.ACTIVE_ROOMS, "W1N1")`.

entries.name: Add, open, close and remove rooms on a private server
entries.title: Add, open, close and remove rooms on a private server
entries.summary: The `map` commands of the server CLI generate new rooms with random terrain, close rooms and reopen them, and delete them. A generated room is open at once and its exits are fitted to its neighbours.

steps.text: `map.generateRoom("E0N3", {sources: 2, terrainType: 2})`. The name must look like `W1N1`; the room must not exist yet.
Wait for `OK`. The command has already written the map images and the terrain cache.
Restart the server, so that the runner and processor processes load the new terrain.
`map.closeRoom("E0N3")` takes it out of play; `map.openRoom("E0N3")` puts it back; `map.openRoom("E0N3", Date.now() + 3600000)` opens it in an hour.
`map.removeRoom("E0N3")` deletes it. After changing terrain by hand, run `map.updateRoomImageAssets("E0N3")` and `map.updateTerrainData()`.

tasks: add a room to the map
open a room at a later time
remove a room from the map
pitfalls: `map.removeRoom` deletes everything in the room, the structures and creeps of players included. There is no confirmation and no undo.
Running runner and processor processes read the terrain cache once, when they start. A room added or removed while they run is unknown to path finding and to player scripts until the server restarts.

A generated room has no `bus` and no `depositType`, so the server never puts power banks or deposits there. For a highway room set them yourself: `storage.db.rooms.update({_id: "E0N3"}, {$set: {bus: true, depositType: "silicon"}})`.
`closeRoom` only sets the status. The terrain cache, in which closed rooms are stored as solid wall, is not rebuilt: run `map.updateTerrainData()` yourself and restart.
Sources, the controller and the mineral are placed inside wall tiles that touch open ground, at random. Look at the result; when it is unusable, remove the room and generate it again.
facts: `generateRoom` refuses a name that does not match `W` or `E`, digits, `N` or `S`, digits, and a room that already exists.

`exits`: an object with `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`, each a list of the open positions along that edge. A side you leave out is copied from the neighbour room, or drawn at random where there is none. A side you give must be equal to the neighbour's, or the command fails.
`terrainType`: 1 to 28, the wall pattern. Left out, a number from 1 to 27 is drawn.
`swampType`: 0 to 14; 0 gives no swamp. Left out, a number from 0 to 13 is drawn.
`sources`: how many sources. Left out, 1 or 2; the README example asks for 4.
`mineral`: a mineral type such as `"H"`, or `false` for none. Left out, a type is drawn from a list where H and O come six times, Z, K, U and L three times and X once.
`controller`: true unless you pass false. `keeperLairs`: false unless you pass true; then every source gets a keeper lair 3 to 5 steps away and the room is marked as a keeper room.
Sources start with 1500 energy and the controller at level 0.
The room is stored with status `normal`: it is in play at once.
`generateRoom` ends by drawing the map images of the room and rebuilding the terrain cache.
`closeRoom` sets the status `out of borders`, and only for a room that is `normal`. `openRoom` sets `normal`.
`openRoom(name, timestamp)` also stores `openTime`, a time in milliseconds. Until then the room stays shut for creeps and for placing spawns.
The list of rooms creeps may enter is rebuilt about every 20 ticks, so opening and closing take a moment to show.
`removeRoom` deletes the room document, all its objects, flags, terrain, pending intents, market statistics, the map view and the map image file.
`updateTerrainData` writes closed rooms into the cache as solid wall.
`updateRoomImageAssets(name)` rewrites the image of the room and the zoomed-out image of the 4 × 4 block around it in the asset folder.

entries.name: NPC bot players on a private server
entries.title: NPC bot players on a private server
entries.summary: A bot is an ordinary user whose code the server loads from a folder. `bots.spawn(aiName, roomName)` creates one with a spawn in a free room; the default world already has four of them running `simplebot`.

steps.text: Register the AI in `mods.json` under `bots`: a name and the folder that holds its `main.js`. Restart the server.
`help(bots)` in the CLI lists the commands and the registered AIs with their folders.
`bots.spawn("simplebot", "W3N1")` creates a bot in that room. Options go in a third argument, e.g. `{username: "Rival", cpu: 200, gcl: 3}`.
After changing files in the folder: `bots.reload("simplebot")`.
`bots.removeUser("RivalBot")` deletes a bot player.

tasks: add a bot to my server
use my own code as a bot
which bots does the server have
pitfalls: `bots.removeUser` deletes the user for good. There is no confirmation and no undo.
It refuses users that are not bots. The test is the `bot` field of the user.
The README lists the option as `name`. The code reads `username`; `name` is ignored.
An AI name that is not in `mods.json` makes `bots.spawn` fail: the list is read when the backend starts.
Files in subfolders of the AI folder are not loaded. Bundle the bot into flat files first.
facts: `bots.spawn` needs a room with a controller that nobody owns.
It creates the user, a code branch `default`, empty memory and a spawn `Spawn1`, and sets the controller to level 1 with 20000 ticks of safe mode.
Options: `username` (default: a random first name followed by `Bot`), `cpu` (100), `gcl` (the level, 1), `x` and `y` of the spawn (a random tile that is not wall).
The code comes from the AI folder: every `.js` file directly in it becomes a module, and `main.js` must be there.
`bots.reload(aiName)` reads the folder again for all users of that AI. The backend does the same for every AI each time it starts.
A bot is a user document with a `bot` field that names its AI. Bots are not counted in the number of players the server reports.
`bots.removeUser(username)` removes the bot's creeps and sites, turns its structures into ruins, frees its controllers, and deletes the user, the code and the memory.
The stock `mods.json` registers one AI, `simplebot`. The default world holds four users that run it.
An npm package with `"screeps_bot": true` whose `main` points at its `main.js` registers itself under its package name when installed in the server folder.
The start room of a bot gets an invader goal of 1,000,000 harvested energy in place of 100,000, so its first raid comes late.

entries.name: Strongholds, invaders, power banks and timed jobs on demand
entries.title: Strongholds, invaders, power banks and timed jobs on demand
entries.summary: NPC content on a private server is made by timed jobs in the backend. From the CLI you can run any job at once, place a stronghold, make one expand, and set the room fields that decide when raids and power banks come.

steps.text: `help(strongholds)` lists the two commands and the templates `bunker1` to `bunker5`.
`strongholds.spawn("W5N5", {templateName: "bunker3"})` places a stronghold in a room that nobody owns.
`strongholds.expand("W5N5")` makes that stronghold put a level 0 core into a room nearby.
Invaders now: insert a creep that belongs to user "2" (the line is under facts), or let the player summon test invaders from the client in an own room.
A power bank now: `storage.db.rooms.update({_id: "W0N5"}, {$set: {powerBankTime: 1}})`, then `system.runCronjob("genPowerBanks")`. The room must be a highway room.
Any other job by name: `system.runCronjob("genDeposits")`, `system.runCronjob("recreateNpcOrders")`.

tasks: why do no invaders come on my server
which cron jobs does the server run
npc market orders on a private server
pitfalls: `strongholds.spawn` never uses `x` and `y` to place the stronghold. With `templateName`, `x` and `y` all given it returns the options and creates nothing; otherwise the place is drawn from the spots where the template fits. Give `templateName` alone.

The raid job leaves out every room that is in the set of active rooms when it runs, and a room with player objects is put back into that set each time it is processed. A raid that is due can therefore take several runs of the job, and `system.runCronjob("genInvaders")` often does nothing for a room with your creeps in it.
No stronghold in the sector means no raids, however much is harvested. On a small or hand-made map check that every sector has one, or place it.

The deposit job picks sector centres with the pattern `^[WE]\d*5[NS]\d*5$` written in a plain string, where `\d` loses its backslash. Read literally it matches only `W5N5`, `E5N5`, `W5S5` and `E5S5`; on a larger map check whether the outer sectors get deposits.
The jobs follow the clock, not the tick. With fast ticks a raid, a power bank or an NPC order comes many ticks after it became due.
Pausing the simulation does not pause the jobs.
A stronghold placed by hand deploys after 1 tick unless you pass `deployTime`; the ones the server makes take 5000.
facts: The jobs and their intervals in seconds are in `config.cronjobs`. The backend looks once a second for jobs that are due; right after a backend start all of them run.
`system.runCronjob(name)` calls the job once more; its regular schedule goes on unchanged.
`strongholds.spawn(roomName, opts)`: `templateName` (`bunker1` to `bunker5`, default random), `user` (default `"2"`, the Invader), `deployTime` (ticks until it becomes active, default 1).
It fails with "room occupied" when the controller of the room has an owner or someone else's reservation, and with "No spots" when the template fits nowhere in the room.
A controller in the room is handed to the stronghold's user at level 8.
At first only the core and ramparts with 1 hit are inserted, and the core cannot be damaged. The engine deploys the stronghold when `deployTime` is reached.
On its own the server gives every sector without a core a stronghold in one of the eight rooms around the sector's centre room, with 5000 ticks until it deploys.

`strongholds.expand(roomName)` needs a core of level 1 or more in that room. It searches outwards through the exits for a room with an unowned controller and no core, and puts a level 0 core within 5 tiles of that controller.

A raid needs all of this: room status `normal`, the room not in the set of active rooms at the moment the job runs, no invader alive in the room, harvested energy at or above the room's `invaderGoal`, a core of level 1 or more in the same sector, and an exit that leads to a room that is neither owned nor reserved.
`invaderGoal: 1` on the room switches the energy test off: `storage.db.rooms.update({_id: "W7N3"}, {$set: {invaderGoal: 1}})`. The other conditions still apply.

An invader by hand, with the small melee body of the raid job: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].insert({type: "creep", user: "2", room: "W7N3", x: 25, y: 25, name: "invader_test", body: ["tough", "tough", "move", "move", "move", "move", "ranged_attack", "work", "attack", "move"].map(type => ({type, hits: 100})), hits: 1000, hitsMax: 1000, fatigue: 0, store: {}, storeCapacity: 0})`. Choose a free, walkable tile. The engine gives every creep of user "2" the invader behaviour and a life of 1500 ticks.
The energy counter is the field `invaderHarvested` of each source; a raid sets it back to 0.
The room in which a player places the first spawn gets `invaderGoal` 1,000,000 instead of 100,000; after the first raid the goal is drawn around 100,000 like everywhere else.
Players can call test invaders into rooms they own or have reserved from the client. The server allows 5 at a time and none while a creep of another player is in the room.

The power bank job serves rooms with `bus: true` and status `normal`. A room gets a bank when its `powerBankTime` has passed; a room without the field first gets a timer of 37,500 to 62,500 ticks and no bank.
The deposit job adds one deposit to a free highway room of a sector as long as the deposits already there, worn by harvesting, yield less than a fixed amount. The type is the room's `depositType`.

Terminals without an owner get new orders every 5000 ticks, give or take 20%: always one sell order for a base mineral, half of the time one for energy, a quarter of the time a buy order for a base mineral.
NPC prices in credits: H and O 3, Z, K, U and L 6, X 18, energy 1. NPC buy orders pay 1. The code holds them in thousandths.

entries.name: Wipe, back up and restore a private server
entries.title: Wipe, back up and restore a private server
entries.summary: The whole world of a stock server is the file `db.json`: copy it while the server is stopped to back up, put the copy back to restore. `system.resetAllData()` replaces everything with the default world, users and their code included.

steps.text: Back up: stop the server, copy `db.json` together with `.screepsrc`, `mods.json`, your mods and the `assets` folder, start again.
Restore: stop the server, put the copied `db.json` and `assets` back, start.
Wipe: in the CLI run `system.resetAllData()`, then restart the server.
Or start clean in a new folder: `npx screeps init` there gives the same default world.

tasks: restore a backup of the server
start over with a fresh map
pitfalls: `system.resetAllData()` deletes every user, all code, all memory and every room change. It does not ask and cannot be undone: copy `db.json` first.
Copy the file with the server stopped. The storage rewrites the whole file every 10 seconds, and a copy taken during a write is not a backup.
With a storage mod the data is not in `db.json`. Back up that database with its own tools.
After a reset players have to sign in and choose a name again; their old user documents are gone with the rest.
facts: `system.resetAllData()` loads the default database that ships with the storage module in place of the current one.
The default world has 121 rooms, `W0N0` to `W10N10`, the users Invader and Source Keeper, and four bot players.
The contributed guide stops and restarts the server right after the reset.
The storage writes the database file every 10 seconds and not when it exits. After the last change wait that long before stopping or copying.
An older `db.json` is upgraded step by step when the storage loads it.
Map images are files in `assets/map`, not part of the database. Back the folder up as well when rooms were generated or removed.
Community practice: when objects are left broken after an unclean stop, administrators repair them with database commands in the CLI; the wiki collects such commands.

entries.name: Get code onto a private server
entries.title: Get code onto a private server
entries.summary: Two ways: let the Steam client sync a local folder, or post the modules to `/api/user/code` on port 21025 over plain HTTP. The second needs a login mod, because the stock server only signs players in through Steam.

steps.text: Simplest: in the Steam client the server has a local script folder; put your build output there and the client uploads it.
For uploads without the client, install a login mod on the server and set a password for your user there.
Post `{branch, modules}` as JSON to `http://<host>:21025/api/user/code` with your tool; with grunt-screeps set `server: {host, port: 21025, http: true}`.
When the server has a password, add the header `X-Server-Password`.

tasks: upload code to a private server
push code to my own server
why does my upload to the private server fail
which port for code upload on a private server
pitfalls: A stock private server speaks plain HTTP on its game port. A tool set up for HTTPS on port 443 does not reach it.
With a server password every upload must also send `X-Server-Password`, or the answer is an error object, not a status code.
Posting to a branch name that does not exist fails with "branch does not exist"; create the branch in the client first.
facts: The route is `POST /api/user/code` with `{branch, modules}`. Without `branch` it writes the branch that is active in the world.
The modules may be 5 MB as JSON at most, and the branch must exist already.
The route wants a token, and the stock server gives tokens only for a Steam ticket. Tools that send e-mail and password need a mod that adds such a login; the contributed Grunt guide says so.
Community practice: the mod used for this is screepsmod-auth.
grunt-screeps takes a `server` object: `host`, `port` and `http: true` make it post over plain HTTP to that address.
Through the Steam client: the client uploads a local folder. The contributed guide copies the build there with rsync, because plain copying gave trouble with the client.
An upload marks the account as active again, and the runner builds a fresh sandbox for the player when it sees newer code.

entries.name: Write a server mod: small examples
entries.title: Write a server mod: small examples
entries.summary: The launcher ships example mods for the usual jobs: change a constant, add a timed job, a CLI command, an HTTP route, a function for player scripts, skip an object type, add an object type with its own command.

steps.text: Create a `.js` file that exports `function(config) { … }` and add its path to `mods` in `mods.json`.
Inside, test for the part of `config` you need (`config.common`, `config.backend`, `config.cli`, `config.cronjobs`, `config.engine`) and change it.
Restart the server. Each process logs the mods it loaded, or the error that stopped one.
Start from the file in `example-mods` that is closest to your job.

tasks: write a mod for my server
change a constant on my server
add a cli command with a mod
add an http endpoint to the server
add a function to the player sandbox
pitfalls: The examples are not switched on: the stock `mods.json` has an empty `mods` list. `mods.example.json` shows the list with all of them.
The tick length a mod sets is ignored once the server has stored its own value. Use `system.setTickDuration`.
A mod runs in every process. Guard each change with the part of `config` it belongs to, or it fails where that part does not exist.
Output of `console.log` goes to the log file of the process, e.g. `logs/backend.log` for a timed job.
facts: Constant: `config.common.constants.CREEP_LIFE_TIME = 300;` inside `if(config.common)`. That part exists in every process, so engine, backend and player scripts agree.
Timed job: `config.cronjobs.myCronJob = [5, function() { … }]`; the number is the interval in seconds.
CLI command: listen to `cliSandbox` on `config.cli` and add a function to the sandbox; what it returns is printed.
HTTP route: `config.backend.router.get("/test", handler)` answers at `/api/test`.
Player sandbox: on `playerSandbox`, `sandbox.run(code)` runs code in the player's global scope, `sandbox.set(name, value)` copies a value in, `sandbox.get(name)` reads one out.
Skip a type: in `processObject` set `object._skip = true`. The example does it for keeper lairs, so no keepers spawn.
Leave users out: wrap `config.engine.driver.getAllUsers` and drop them from its result.
Welcome text: `config.backend.welcomeText`, with HTML. It is part of the server info every client fetches.
E-mail: listen to `sendUserNotifications` on `config.backend` and send the list yourself. The example uses nodemailer and skips users without `email`.

New object type: `config.engine.registerCustomObjectPrototype(type, className, opts)` gives documents of that `type` a class in player scripts. `opts` may hold `properties` (name to function of the raw document), `prototypeExtender(prototype, scope)`, `userOwned`, `findConstant`, `lookConstant`, `parent`.
The functions in `opts` are turned into text and run inside the player sandbox. They cannot use variables of the mod file.
Players get the objects with `room.find(findConstant)`; the examples use 10000.
Logic per tick for the type goes into `processObject`: `objectsUpdate.update(object, {counter: object.counter + 1})`.
A command for the type: the method added in `prototypeExtender` calls `scope.intents.set(this.id, name, data)`; the mod carries it out in `processObjectIntents`.
A new intent name must be declared with the type of each field in `config.engine.customIntentTypes`, e.g. `{incValue: "number"}`. Only declared names and fields get through.
Field types: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `price`, `string[]`, `number[]`, `bodypart[]`, `userString` (cut at 100 characters), `userText` (cut at 1000).
An instance is made by inserting a document: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].insert({type: "myobject", room: "W1N1", x: 20, y: 20})`.

entries.name: Draw a custom object in the client
entries.title: Draw a custom object in the client
entries.summary: A mod tells clients how to draw an object type by putting renderer metadata into `config.backend.renderer.metadata[type]`: a list of processors (draw, sprite, text) with optional calculations and actions.

steps.text: In the mod, under `if(config.backend)`, set `config.backend.renderer.metadata["mytype"] = {processors: [ … ]}`.
Simplest drawing: one processor `{type: "draw", once: true, payload: {drawings: [ … ]}}`; each drawing is a method of a PIXI Graphics object with its parameters.

For an image: `config.backend.renderer.resources["name"] = "{ASSETS_URL}/file.png"`, put the file into the asset folder, and use a processor `{type: "sprite", payload: {texture: "name", width, height}}`.
To follow a field of the object, add `props: ["score"]` to the processor and read the value with `{$state: "score"}`.
Insert an object of the type from the CLI and look at the room.

tasks: show a sprite for my object type
side panel for a custom object
pitfalls: The metadata travels to the client as JSON. Write conditions and values as expressions; a JavaScript function in mod metadata does not arrive.
Drawing and scripting are separate. Metadata only draws; `config.engine.registerCustomObjectPrototype` is what gives player scripts a class for the type.
facts: The backend sends `config.backend.renderer` (its `resources` and `metadata`) and `customObjectTypes` to clients as part of the server info.
Metadata of a type: `processors`, and optionally `calculations`, `actions`, `zIndex`, `texture`, `data`, `disappearProcessor`.
Processors that create something: `draw` (Graphics calls listed in `payload.drawings`), `sprite` (`payload.texture`), `text` (`payload.text`, `payload.style`), `container`, `object`.
The examples work in units of 100 per tile with the tile centre at 0, 0: a circle of radius 40, a sprite 100 wide, a position factor of 100.
Keys that steer when something runs, on processors, calculations and actions: `once`, `props` (run again when one of these fields changes), `when` and `until` (conditions).

An expression is an object with a key that starts with `$`: `$state` reads a field of the game object, `$calc` the result of a calculation, `$processorParam` a parameter such as `tickDuration`, `$rel` a property of the drawn object.
Expressions combine with `$if` (`then`, `else`), `$and`, `$or`, `$not`, `$eq`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$add`, `$sub`, `$mul`, `$div`, `$min`, `$max`, `$concat`.
A calculation has an `id`, `props` and a `func`; processors read it with `{$calc: id}`. The example computes a radius from `score` and `scoreMax`.
Layers from bottom to top: `terrain`, `objects` (the default), `lighting`, `effects`. A processor chooses one with `layer`; the examples put a `glow` texture on `lighting`.

Actions animate a drawn object: `Repeat`, `Sequence`, `Spawn` (in parallel), `ScaleTo`, `MoveTo`, `RotateTo`, `TintTo`, `AlphaTo`, `FadeIn`, `FadeOut`, `Blink`, `DelayTime`, and `…By` forms. Durations are in seconds.
An action list directly in the metadata can aim at a processor by `targetId` and have its own `when`.
Image files: the placeholder `{ASSETS_URL}` in a resource path stands for the server's `/assets` address, which serves the asset folder. `gift.png` is in the default assets for the examples.
Side panel: `config.backend.customObjectTypes[type] = {sidepanel: html}`. The HTML may show fields of the object through placeholders in double braces around `object.<field>`.
The renderer repository holds a demo app and the metadata of every stock object type to copy from.
Test object: `storage.db["rooms.objects"].insert({type: "test", room: "W3N3", x: 20, y: 20})`; change a field with `update` and the drawing follows.

entries.name: Store and serve room history (replays)
entries.title: Store and serve room history (replays)
entries.summary: The engine hands out room history in chunks of 20 ticks, but the stock server keeps none. A mod has to save each chunk on the `saveRoomHistory` event and return it from `config.backend.onGetRoomHistory`.

steps.text: In a mod, under `if(config.engine)`: `config.engine.on("saveRoomHistory", (roomName, baseTime, data) => { … })` and store `data` under room and base tick.
Under `if(config.backend)`: `config.backend.onGetRoomHistory = (roomName, baseTime, callback) => { … }` and call back with `(error, text)`.
Add the mod to `mods.json` and restart. The example `room-history.js` does both with JSON files.

tasks: enable room history on my server
why is there no history on my server
save room history with a mod
pitfalls: The example never deletes anything: every active room adds a file every 20 ticks. Add a clean-up of old chunks.
The example calls `fs.writeFile` without a callback. The Node versions the server now needs throw on that; pass a callback before using the file.
The two halves run in different processes: saving in the processors, serving in the backend. They must reach the same files or database.
facts: Every tick the processor stores the objects of each active room in the key-value store. Every `historyChunkSize` ticks, 20, the driver puts the previous chunk together, emits it as `saveRoomHistory` and drops the stored ticks.
A chunk is an object with `timestamp`, `room`, `base` and `ticks`. The first tick holds all objects, each later tick only what changed.
History is recorded only for rooms that stay active, such as rooms with player objects.
A client asks `/room-history?room=…&time=…`. The backend passes room and time to `config.backend.onGetRoomHistory`; the stock function answers "not implemented", which the client gets as status 500.
The example mod writes one file per chunk, `replay-data/<room>/<base tick>.json` next to the mod file, and reads it back on request.
The chunk size exists twice and must agree: `config.engine.historyChunkSize` cuts the chunks, `config.backend.historyChunkSize` is what clients are told.

entries.title: Community launcher and the usual mods
entries.summary: Community practice: public private servers are mostly started with a community launcher in Docker and run a handful of community mods for password login, more admin commands, a real database and room history. Pointers only; each mod has its own documentation.

steps.text: Community practice: start the server with a community launcher or Docker image rather than the bare npm package; the launcher takes care of the dependencies.
Add the mods that fill the gaps you care about: login with a password, admin commands, MongoDB storage, history.
Say in the welcome text what you changed.
For the list of community servers in the client: meet the official rules, then write to the developers.

get my server on the community server list
pitfalls: The contributed guide is from 2018 and names Ubuntu 16 and Node 8. The mod names still help; the versions do not, the current server needs Node 22.
After changing the storage with a mod the new database is empty: the guide fills it with `system.resetAllData()` and restarts.
A mod is loaded into the server processes with all their rights: database, files, network. Install only mods whose code you trust.
facts: Community practice: most servers are started with a community launcher, usually in Docker, instead of installing the npm package by hand.

The contributed official guide installs five community mods: screepsmod-mongo (storage in MongoDB and Redis), screepsmod-auth (a password for tools), screepsmod-tickrate (tick rate from the CLI), screepsmod-admin-utils (more CLI functions), screepsmod-features (tells clients what the server supports).
Community practice: further mods cover room history, an NPC market and CPU that grows with GCL.
The stock server sets the tick length from the CLI by itself, with `system.setTickDuration`.

To be shown in the client's list of community servers: server version 4.0.0 or higher, stable for the last 7 days, and a `welcomeText` that tells players about customisations and mods. The request goes to the developers by e-mail.

entries.name: From the first spawn to room level 4
entries.title: From the first spawn to room level 4
entries.summary: What to build and which creeps to run at each room level, from one spawn in an empty room to a storage at level 4.

steps.text: Level 1, 300 energy per creep: workers of [WORK, CARRY, MOVE] (200) or [WORK, WORK, CARRY, MOVE] (300) that harvest, fill the spawn and upgrade. The spawn adds 1 energy per tick by itself while the room holds less than 300.
Level 2 costs only 200 energy: upgrade first, build after.
Level 2: 5 extensions (3000 each) lift spawn energy to 550. A container (5000) at each source. Walls and ramparts become available.
With that energy: one miner of 5 WORK + 1 MOVE (550) per source takes all of its 10 energy per tick. Haulers of CARRY and MOVE carry it; the first workers go on as builders and upgraders.
Level 3 (45,000 energy): 5 more extensions (spawn energy 800) and the first tower (5000).
Fill the tower (1000 energy, 10 per action) and keep it filled: it is the answer to invader raids.
Roads from the sources to the spawn and the controller: 300 per plain tile, 1500 per swamp tile. On roads a loaded creep needs half the MOVE parts.
Level 4 (135,000 energy): 10 more extensions (spawn energy 1300) and the storage (30,000, holds 1,000,000).
From level 2 on, ramparts over spawn and tower: 1 energy to build, then repair at once.

what to build at room level 2
build order for a new room
start a room from one spawn
pitfalls: The first room starts in safe mode for 20000 ticks. Towers come at level 3, so that is the time to reach it.
Only the first spawn, placed by hand, starts with 300 energy and costs nothing. A spawn in a later room is built for 15,000 and starts empty.
Upgrade over many ticks, not in a few big ones: the level only rises while the downgrade timer is full, and a tick with an upgrade adds only 100 ticks to it. After a level-up it starts at half.
Sites count against the room level like finished structures: a sixth extension site at level 2 returns ERR_RCL_NOT_ENOUGH.
A new rampart has 1 hit and is gone after 100 ticks unless it has been repaired above 300 hits by then.
Each level gained adds one safe mode to the stock.
At level 2 the downgrade timer is the shortest of all: 10,000 ticks.

entries.name: Defend a room: ramparts, towers, repair, safe mode
entries.title: Defend a room: ramparts, towers, repair, safe mode
entries.summary: Defence of an owned room in layers: ramparts over what must survive, towers that fire when it pays, repair under fire, and safe mode as the last step.

steps.text: Ramparts (1 energy each) on spawn, storage, terminal and towers, and on the tiles where your defenders will stand. A rampart may share its tile with any structure.
Lift every new rampart above 300 hits within 100 ticks, then raise all of them evenly: 0.01 energy per hit, up to 3,000,000 at level 4 and 300,000,000 at level 8.
Every tick: FIND_HOSTILE_CREEPS. Count their HEAL, ATTACK, RANGED_ATTACK and WORK parts; creep.body also shows the boosts.
All towers on one target, when their summed damage at its range beats its healing: 600 per tower up to range 5, 150 from range 20. A HEAL part restores 12, with XLHO2 48.
Melee defenders stand on ramparts next to the tile under attack: nothing reaches them until the rampart falls, and they take no hit-back.
Towers heal defenders that are hit: 400 close, 100 far.
A rampart that is being broken: 800 hits per tower action close, 200 far; repair creeps add 100 hits per WORK part per tick. A tower that repairs does not shoot in that tick.
Keep the towers fed: a full tower has 100 actions, and below 10 energy it does nothing.
Last step, when a rampart over spawn, storage or towers is about to fall: 20,000 ticks in which hostile creeps can do nothing. Needs stock, no cooldown, and a controller that is not upgrade-blocked.

tasks: defend my room against another player
when to activate safe mode in a fight
stop an attack on my room
pitfalls: One attackController on your controller takes safe mode away for 1000 ticks. Keep CLAIM creeps from reaching the controller (walls or ramparts around it), or activate before they arrive.
Safe mode also fails when the downgrade timer is more than 5000 ticks below half of its maximum: a room you do not upgrade cannot be saved this way.
A public rampart lets hostile creeps onto it and then shields them from your towers. Close ramparts while hostiles are in the room.
rangedMassAttack cannot hurt what stands under a rampart, but it wears down every rampart within range 3 at once.
Calling attack, heal and repair on the same tower in one tick runs only one of them (heal, else repair, else attack) and costs the CPU of all three.
A spawn boxed in by enemy creeps frees itself: when its creep is ready and no tile is free, one enemy creep next to it is killed.
Hostile creeps destroy your construction sites by walking over them. Rebuild inside the ramparts first.

entries.name: Attack a room: towers, healing, breaking in, the controller
entries.title: Attack a room: towers, healing, breaking in, the controller
entries.summary: What an attack on an owned room must survive and do: tower damage by range and number of towers, the healing that matches it, the time to break a rampart, and what CLAIM parts do to the controller.

steps.text: Scout first: number and position of towers, rampart hits, and on the controller level, safeMode, safeModeAvailable and safeModeCooldown.
Count the damage: a tower does 600 at range 5 or less, falling to 150 at range 20 and more. A level 8 room has 6: 3600 to 900 per tick on one creep.

Bring healing that matches it: 12 per HEAL part on an adjacent creep, 4 at range 3; XLHO2 gives 48 and 16. Damage and healing of a tick are netted, so a creep lives if it never falls to 0 within one tick.
Body order: TOUGH first (with XGHO2 it takes ×0.3 damage while those parts have hits), working parts next, HEAL and MOVE last.
Break in at range 1: 50 hits per WORK part per tick (XZH2O ×4), or 30 per ATTACK part (XUH2O ×4); 10 per RANGED_ATTACK part from range 3. A rampart on the tile takes all of it first.
Targets inside: towers, then spawns (a spawn destroyed while spawning loses the creep in it), then storage and terminal.
CLAIM creeps at the controller: each part takes 300 ticks off the downgrade timer, and the hit blocks upgrading, safe mode and further hits for 1000 ticks. All parts have to hit in the same tick.
At level 0 the room is neutral: claim it, reserve it or leave it. The old structures stay and no longer work.

tasks: how much healing to survive towers
how many HEAL parts against towers
tower damage an attacker takes at each range
how long to dismantle a rampart
pitfalls: In a room under the defender's safe mode attack, rangedAttack, dismantle, heal and attackController return ERR_NO_BODYPART. Read controller.safeMode before you enter, and expect an activation as soon as you do damage, unless the controller is upgrade-blocked.

One wave of n CLAIM parts costs the controller n × 300 ticks, plus the 1000 ticks that run off while the owner cannot upgrade. A full level 8 timer is 200,000 ticks; after each lost level it restarts at half of the lower level's maximum.
CLAIM creeps live 600 ticks and cannot be renewed: every wave needs new ones.
Melee against a creep costs you its ATTACK parts back in damage, unless you stand on a rampart. Dismantle and ranged attacks draw no hit-back.
Overkill on a rampart is lost: what is under it survives the tick in which the rampart falls.
Do not surround an enemy spawn with single creeps: when it has a creep ready and no free tile, it kills one of yours.
A drained tower is harmless: under 10 energy it cannot act. A full one has 100 actions.

entries.name: Upgrading at room level 8
entries.title: Upgrading at room level 8
entries.summary: A level 8 controller takes 15 energy per tick from all creeps together. One upgrader with 15 WORK parts uses the whole cap; only boosts and a power creep go above it.

steps.text: One upgrader with 15 WORK parts (1 energy per WORK per tick) spends the whole cap. More WORK on the controller does nothing.
Feed it from a link or container within range 1, so it never walks: 15 energy per tick, 22,500 per creep life.
Range 3, every tick. Each point also counts for GCL; controller.progress stays 0.
Boosts multiply the points, not the energy: XGH2O makes 30 points from the same 15 energy, for 450 compound and 300 energy per creep.
PWR_OPERATE_CONTROLLER raises the cap by 10 to 50 energy per tick for 1000 ticks; size the upgrader for the raised cap.
The timer holds 200,000 ticks and every tick with an upgrade adds 100. Below 95,000 safe mode can no longer be activated.

how many WORK parts for a level 8 upgrader
raise GCL with a level 8 room
keep a level 8 controller from downgrading
is boosting upgraders worth it at level 8
pitfalls: The cap is shared and used up in processing order: once it is reached, the upgradeController calls of the other creeps do nothing, although they returned OK and cost 0.2 CPU each.
The cap counts energy, before boosts: a boosted upgrader still needs only 15 WORK parts.
GCL gets the boosted points, rounded down per creep and tick.
progressTotal is undefined at level 8 and progress stays 0: do not steer upgraders by them.
After an attackController hit nobody can upgrade for 1000 ticks and the timer runs down meanwhile.
If the timer does run out the room drops to level 7, and the structures above the level 7 allowance stop working until level 8 is reached again.

entries.name: Keep ramparts up
entries.title: Keep ramparts up
entries.summary: Each rampart loses 300 hits every 100 ticks. Repair new ones at once, hold all of them above a floor with a repair creep, and keep the towers for emergencies.

steps.text: FIND_MY_STRUCTURES filtered by STRUCTURE_RAMPART; walls are in FIND_STRUCTURES, they have no owner. Work on the one with the fewest hits.
A finished rampart has 1 hit and 100 ticks until its first loss of 300: the builder repairs it straight away, well above that.
Repair creep: 100 hits per WORK part per tick for 1 energy, range 3. One WORK part that repairs all the time offsets the decay of 33 ramparts.
Budget: 0.03 energy per rampart per tick, so 3 per tick for 100 ramparts.
Tower only below an emergency floor: 800 hits up to range 5, 200 from range 20, for 10 energy.
Raise the floor with spare energy, up to hitsMax of the room level. Skip ramparts that are at hitsMax.

pitfalls: A rampart with 300 hits or fewer is removed at its next decay, whatever stands under it.
repair on a rampart at hitsMax returns OK, does nothing and costs the 0.2 CPU.
hitsMax follows the room level every tick. At level 1, or once the room is no longer yours, it is 0: repair has no effect and the ramparts decay away.

A tower that repairs does not shoot in the same tick.

entries.summary: What your creeps can do depends on who owns or reserved the room, and on whether the target has an owner. Roads, containers and walls have no owner.
tasks: what can I do in a room I do not own

facts: harvest a source: yes in your own, your reserved and neutral rooms; ERR_NOT_OWNER in a room owned or reserved by someone else (an invader core reservation included).
createConstructionSite: your rooms (by room level); neutral rooms and rooms you reserved (roads and up to 5 containers); never in a room owned or reserved by someone else.
build, repair: any site or structure in any room. Neither checks the owner.
transfer, pickup: anywhere, into anyone's creeps and structures.

withdraw: from containers, tombstones, ruins and another player's structures in any room, except where a closed rampart of another player covers a target that is not yours (a container counts as not yours). Never in a room under another player's safe mode.

dismantle, attack, rangedAttack: structures of any owner in any room, except in a room under another player's safe mode; dismantle only works on structure types that can be built (not an invader core or a power bank). A rampart on the tile takes the damage first.
Structure.destroy(): only in a room whose controller you own, on any structure there, and only while no creep of another user is in the room.
ConstructionSite.remove(): your own sites anywhere; other players' sites only in your room. Walking onto another player's site also removes it.

reserveController: controller without owner and without someone else's reservation. claimController: the same, plus a free GCL slot. upgradeController: your controller only. signController: any controller.
